Question 134. You have been appointed as the statutory auditor of a limited company. The company is registered as a Nidhi company. What are the reporting requirements of a Nidhi company under the Companies Auditor's Report Order, 2020?

(4 Marks| 5 Minutes) (RTP May 24)(Medium)

Answer 134. Reporting requirements of a Nidhi Company under the CARO 2020: The auditor is required to report under clause (xii) of Paragraph 3 of CARO 2020: a) Whether the Nidhi Company has complied with the Net Owned Funds to Deposits in the ratio of 1:20 to meet out the liability; b) Whether the Nidhi Company is maintaining ten per cent. unencumbered term deposits as specified in the Nidhi Rules, 2014 to meet out the liability; c) Whether there has been any default in payment of interest on deposits or repayment thereof for any period and if so, the details thereof.

Approach & time saving tips

1. Explain significant deficiency concept first.
2. Mention written communication to management/TCWG.
3. Use practical internal control examples.

Examiner observation

1. Students confuse deficiencies with audit qualification.
2. Timing and recipient of communication are often missed.
3. SA 265 terminology should be used properly.

Question 135. SKN Ltd. a biopharma company and global manufacturers of select critical care medical products has been sanctioned working capital limits of ₹ 5.99 crores from a nationalized bank on the basis of security of current assets. During the year under audit, the statutory auditor of SKN Ltd. considers that inventory is material to the financial statements and performs audit procedures over the company's final inventory records to determine whether they accurately reflect actual inventory count and without any major discrepancies for each class of inventory. What are the reporting requirements regarding physical verification of inventory under CARO 2020 in this case?

(4 Marks| 5 Minutes) (MTP-I Mar.25)(Medium)

Answer 135. As per clause (ii) of Paragraph 3 of CARO, 2020 the auditor is required to report, in respect of physical verification of inventory and in respect of sanctioned working capital, that: (i) Whether physical verification of inventory has been conducted at reasonable intervals by the management and whether, in the opinion of the auditor, the coverage and procedure of such verification by the management is appropriate; whether any discrepancies of 10% or more in the aggregate for each class of inventory were noticed and if so, whether they have been properly dealt with in the books of account.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 566

(ii) Whether during any point of time of the year, the company has been sanctioned working capital limits in excess of five crore rupees, in aggregate, from banks or financial institutions on the basis of security of current assets; whether the quarterly returns or statements filed by the company with such banks or financial institutions are in agreement with the books of account of the Company, if not, give details.

Approach & time saving tips

1. Focus on impact of computerised systems on audit evidence.
2. Mention internal controls and CAATs separately.
3. Use practical ERP/software examples.

Examiner observation

1. Students write only theory of computers.
2. Audit trail and access controls are often omitted.
3. Risk-based approach is preferred.

Question 136. Discuss the reporting requirements as per CARO, 2020, regarding: (i) Statutory Dues (ii) Transactions with Related Parties

(5 Marks| 5 Minutes) (RTP Sept.24)(Medium)

Answer 136. (i) Reporting under CARO,2020 regarding statutory Dues [Para 3(vii)] a) Whether the company is regular in depositing undisputed statutory dues including Goods and Services Tax, provident fund, employees' state insurance, income tax, sales-tax, service tax, duty of customs, duty of excise, value added tax, cess and any other statutory dues to the appropriate authorities and if not, the extent of the arrears of outstanding statutory dues as on the last day of the financial year concerned for a period of more than six months from the date they became payable, shall be indicated; b) Where statutory dues referred to in sub-clause (a) have not been deposited on account of any dispute, then the amounts involved and the forum where dispute is pending shall be mentioned (a mere representation to the concerned Department shall not be treated as a dispute); (ii) Reporting under CARO, 2020 regarding transactions with related parties [Para 3(xiii)] Whether all transactions with the related parties are in compliance with sections 177 and 188 of Companies Act where applicable and the details have been disclosed in the financial statements, etc., as required by the applicable accounting standards.

Approach & time saving tips

1. Define CAATs briefly and give examples like audit software/test data.
2. Mention advantages such as speed and large data testing.
3. Use point-wise presentation.

Examiner observation

1. Students fail to explain practical use of CAATs.
2. Difference between test data and audit software is often unclear.
3. Application-oriented answers score better.

Question 137. CA Student Manoj is studying on the exemptions available to a private limited company in respect of certain reporting requirements. You are required to guide Manoj on the following: (i) Applicability of ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 567

Reporting requirements on adequacy of Internal Financial Controls (IFCs) with reference to financial statements to a private limited company. (ii) Applicability of Companies (Auditor's Report) Order, 2020 to a private limited company.

(4 marks|6 minutes)[Easy|ICAI Fav]

Answer: (i) Applicability of Reporting requirements on adequacy of IFC w.r.t to financial statements to a Private Limited Company: The auditor’s report shall state whether the company has adequate Internal financial controls with reference to financial statements in place and also on the operating effectiveness of such controls. This requirement shall not apply to a private company which – I) Is a One Person Company or a small company; or II) Has turnover less than ₹ 50 crore as per the latest audited Financial Statements, and which has aggregate borrowings from banks or financial institutions or any body corporate at any point of time during the financial Year less than ₹ 25 crore. (ii) Applicability of CARO to a Private Limited Company: Companies (Auditor’s Report) Order, 2020 shall not apply to a private limited company, not being a subsidiary or holding company of a public company: I) Having a paid-up capital and reserves and surplus not more than ₹ 1 crore as on the balance sheet date and II) Does not have total borrowings exceeding ₹ 1 crore from any bank or financial institution at any point of time during the financial year and III) Does not have a total revenue as disclosed in Scheduled III to the Companies Act (including revenue from discontinuing operations) exceeding ₹ 10 crore during the financial year as per the financial statements.

Approach & time saving tips Write the conditions in bullet points rather than lengthy paragraphs. Mention that the private company should not be a subsidiary/holding of a public company for CARO exemption. Divide the answer into Part (i) IFC Reporting and Part (ii) CARO Applicability. Start each part with the relevant legal provision and then list the exemption conditions point-wise.

Examiner observation Students often interchange the limits prescribed for IFC reporting and CARO exemption. Many forget to mention that CARO exemption is available only when the private company is not a subsidiary or holding company of a public company.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 568

(Multiple Choices Questions) MCQ

Question 1. Eeyore Pvt. Ltd. is incorporated on 1st July, 2017. During the Financial Year ending on 31set March, 2018, the company did not opt for any borrowing at any point of time and have a total revenue of Rs. 60 Lakh. At the year end, it provides the following information regarding its paid-up capital and reserve & surplus- Particulars Amount (in Rs.) Paid-up Capital Consideration received in cash for equity shares (including unpaid calls of Rs. 5,00,000) 40,00,000 Consideration received in cash for preference shares 25,00,000 Bonus shares allotted 7,00,000 Share application money received pending allotment 10,00,000 Sub-Total 82,00,000 Reserve & Surplus Balance in Statement of Profit and Loss 15,00,000 Capital Reserves 10,00,000 Sub-Total 25,00,000 GRAND TOTAL 1,07,00,000 You are provided with the provisions regarding applicability of Companies (Auditor’ s Report) Order, 2016, (CARO, 2020) issued under section 143(11) of the Companies Act, 2013 to a private limited company that it specifically exempts a private limited company having a paid up capital and reserves and surplus not more than Rs. 1 crore as on the Balance Sheet date and which does not have total borrowings exceeding Rs. 1 crore from any bank at any point of time during the financial year and which does not have a total revenue as disclosed in Scheduled III to the Companies Act, 2013 exceeding Rs. 10 crore during the financial year. Considering the information given above, which of the following shall be considered as a reason regarding applicability or non-applicability of CARO, 2016 (CARO 2020)? (a) Reporting under CARO, 2016 (CARO 2020) shall be applicable as the company is having a paid up capital and reserves and surplus of Rs. 1.07 crore i.e. more than Rs. 1 crore as on the Balance Sheet date. (b) Reporting under CARO, 2016 (CARO 2020) shall be applicable as the company is having a paid up capital and reserves and surplus of Rs. 1.02 crore i.e. more than Rs. 1 crore as on the Balance Sheet date. (c) Reporting under CARO, 2016 (CARO 2020) shall not be applicable as the company is having a paid up capital and reserves and surplus of Rs. 0.92 crore i.e. not more than Rs. 1 crore as on the Balance Sheet date. (d) Reporting under CARO, 2016 (CARO 2020) shall not be applicable as the company is having a paid up capital and reserves and surplus of Rs. 0.82 crore i.e. not more than Rs. 1 crore as on the Balance Sheet data.

(RTP May ‘19)

Ans: (c) Reporting under CARO, 2016 (CARO 2020) shall not be applicable as the company is having a paid up capital and reserves and surplus of Rs. 0.92 crore i.e. not more than Rs. 1 crore as on the Balance Sheet date. Reason: CARO, 2016 is not applicable because: Paid-up capital + Reserves & Surplus = Rs. 92 lakh (less than Rs. 1 crore) No borrowings during the year Total revenue = Rs. 60 lakh (less than Rs. 10 crore)

Question 2. For which of following company, provisions of CARO,2020 would be applicable? ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 569

(a) Boost Up Training (OPC) Private Limited (b) RCI Bank Limited (c) PST Industries Limited (d) Moon Insurance Limited

(MTP Oct ’23)

Ans: (c) Reason: CARO, 2020 is applicable to all companies except the following: One Person Company (OPC) → ❌ (Exempt) Banking company → ❌ (Exempt) Insurance company → ❌ (Exempt) Only PST Industries Ltd. is a regular company (not OPC, bank, or insurer), so CARO, 2020 applies to it. CARO, 2020 applicable to: PST Industries Limited

Question 3. In case of a fraud involving less than Rs. 1 crore, the auditor shall (a) report the matter to the audit committee constituted under section 177 or to the Board in other cases within such time and in such manner as prescribed. (b) report the matter to the audit committee constituted under section 177 within such time and in such manner as prescribed. (c) report the matter to the Board within such time and in such manner as prescribed. (d) report the matter to the audit committee constituted under section 177 and also to the Board within such time and in such manner as prescribed.

(MTP March ’19)

Ans: (a) report the matter to the audit committee constituted under section 177 or to the Board in other cases within such time and in such manner as prescribed. Reason: As per Section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013 (read with related rules): If the auditor detects a fraud involving less than Rs. 1 crore, they must report it to the Audit Committee (if constituted under section 177) or to the Board in other cases. Hence, option (a) is correct as it covers both scenarios

Question 4. During the course of audit of a listed company, CA P finds that solar power generating plant capitalized in books for Rs.5.00 crore during the year does not exist. It became known that only bills were arranged and no assets were actually procured. Besides, financial statements also reflect depreciation of Rs.1.50 core on above. The bills of capitalized asset were approved by procurement head. The matter was reported to audit committee by CA P. However, no response was received. Considering above, choose the most appropriate option: - (a) The matter needs to be reported to MCA in ADT-4. It also requires reporting under CARO,2020. (b) The matter needs to be reported to MCA in ADT-4. It does not require reporting under CARO,2020. (c) The matter need not be reported to MCA. However, it requires reporting under CARO,2020. (d) The matter needs neither reporting to MCA nor under CARO,2020

(MTP Oct’22)

Ans: (a) The matter needs to be reported to MCA in ADT-4. It also requires reporting under CARO,2020.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 570

Reason: The capitalization of a non-existent asset using fake bills is a case of fraud by company personnel (procurement head). As per Section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013, fraud involving Rs. 1 crore or more must be reported to the MCA in Form ADT-4. Under CARO, 2020, Clause 3(xi)(A) requires the auditor to report any fraud noticed or reported during the year. Hence, the fraud must be reported both to the MCA and under CARO, 2020.

Question 5. While reporting under CARO, 2020, it is duty of statutory auditor of company to report: (a) Fraud of less than Rs. 1 crore committed by officers or employees of company during the year (b) Fraud of Rs.1 crore or more committed by officers or employees of company during the year (c) Fraud of Rs.5 crore or more committed by officers or employees of company during the year (d) Any fraud by the company or on the company noticed or reported during the year

(MTP Oct ’23)

Ans: (d) Any fraud by the company or on the company noticed or reported during the year Reason: As per Clause 3(xi)(A) of CARO, 2020, the statutory auditor must report: “Any fraud by the company or on the company noticed or reported during the year.” There is no monetary threshold specified under CARO for this reporting. The focus is on the existence of fraud, whether big or small. Hence, (d) is correct — auditor must report any fraud noticed or reported during the year

Question 6. To jointly audit books of accounts of WZ Limited for the financial year 2020-21 two different firms of Chartered Accountants namely MH and Associates and NR and Associates were appointed. MH and Associates and NR and Associates can together be called as: (a) Principal Auditors of WZ Limited. (b) Branch Auditors of WZ Limited. (c) Individual Auditors of WZ Limited. (d) Joint Auditors of WZ Limited.

(RTP Nov ’21)

Ans: (d) Joint Auditors of WZ Limited. Reason: When two or more audit firms are appointed to conduct the audit of the same entity for the same period, they are termed as Joint Auditors as per SA 299 (Revised) – Responsibility of Joint Auditors. MH and Associates and NR and Associates auditing WZ Limited together = Joint Auditors.

Question 7. Which of the following is not an advantage of Joint Audit: (a) Sharing of expertise. (b) General superiority complexes of some auditors. (c) Lower workload. (d) Displacement of the auditor of the company taken over in a take – over often obviated.

(MTP Oct 19)

Ans: (b) General superiority complexes of some auditors.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 571

Reason: "General superiority complexes" among auditors is a disadvantage, not an advantage. It can lead to lack of coordination, conflicts, or inefficiency in a joint audit. Hence, option (b) is not an advantage of joint audit.

Question 8. Which of the following is correct, in case of joint audit, where there is disagreement with regard to the opinion or any matters to be covered by the audit report. (a) The auditors shall express their opinion in separate audit report. (b) The audit report(s) issued by the joint auditor(s) shall make a reference to each other’s audit report(s). (c) Both (a) and (b) are correct (d) The auditor who is having a separate opinion is bound by the opinion of the majority of the auditors and needs to issue a common audit report.

(MTP March ‘21)

Ans: (c) Both (a) and (b) are correct Reason: As per SA 299 (Revised) on Joint Audit of Financial Statements: If joint auditors disagree on any matter, each can issue a separate audit report stating their own opinion (✔⮚ option a). In such a case, each report should make reference to the other auditor’s report (✔⮚option b). Hence, both (a) and (b) are correct in case of disagreement.

Question 9. Which of the following is correct: (a) When reporting on prior period financial statements in connection with the current period’s audit, if the auditor’s opinion on such prior period financial statements differs from the opinion the auditor previously expressed, the auditor need not disclose the substantive reasons for the different opinion. (b) When reporting on prior period financial statements in connection with the current period’s audit, if the auditor’s opinion on such prior period financial statements differs from the opinion the auditor previously expressed, the auditor shall disclose the substantive reasons for the different opinion in an Other Matter paragraph in accordance with SA 706. (c) When reporting on prior period financial statements in connection with the current period’s audit, if the auditor’s opinion on such prior period financial statements differs from the opinion the auditor previously expressed, the auditor shall disclose the substantive reasons for the different opinion in an emphasis of Matter paragraph in accordance with SA 706. (d) When reporting on prior period financial statements in connection with the current period’s audit, if the auditor’s opinion on such prior period financial statements differs from the opinion the auditor previously expressed, the auditor shall disclose the substantive reasons for the different opinion in an Other Matter paragraph or emphasis of matter paragraph in accordance with SA 706. (MTP April 19)

Ans: (b) When reporting on prior period financial statements in connection with the current period’s audit, if the auditor’s opinion on such prior period financial statements differs from the opinion the auditor previously expressed, the auditor shall disclose the substantive reasons for the different opinion in an Other Matter paragraph in accordance with SA 706.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 572

Reason: As per SA 706 (Revised), when the auditor’s opinion on prior period financial statements differs from the opinion previously expressed, the auditor shall disclose the substantive reasons for the difference in an Other Matter paragraph in the current auditor’s report. Other Matter paragraph is specifically used to communicate such information. Emphasis of Matter paragraph is not appropriate for this purpose. Hence, option (b) is correct.

Question10. CA. Goofy has been appointed as an auditor for audit of a complete set of financial statements of Dippy Ltd., a listed company. The financial statements of the company are prepared by the management in accordance with the Accounting Standards prescribed under section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013. However, the inventories are m isstated which is deemed to be material but not pervasive to the financial statements. Based on the audit evidences obtained, CA. Goofy has concluded that a material uncertainty does not exist related to events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on the entity’s ability to continue as a going concern in accordance with SA 570. Further, CA. Goofy is also aware of the fact that a qualified opinion would be appropriate due to a material misstatement of the Financial Statements. State what phrases should the auditor use while drafting such opinion paragraph? (a) In our opinion and to the best of our information and according to the explanations given to us, except for the effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section of our report, the aforesaid financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, or give a true and fair view in conformity with the applicable financial reporting framework. (b) In our opinion and to the best of our information and according to the explanations given to us, with the foregoing explanation, the aforesaid financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, or give a true and fair view in conformity with the applicable financial reporting framework. (c) In our opinion and to the best of our information and according to the explanations given to us, subject to the misstatement regarding inventories, the aforesaid financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, or give a true and fair view in conformity with the applicable financial reporting framework. (d) In our opinion and to the best of our information and according to the explanations given to us, with the explanation described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section of our report, the aforesaid financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, or give a true and fair view in conformity with the applicable financial reporting framework.

(RTP May ‘19)

Ans: (a) In our opinion and to the best of our information and according to the explanations given to us, except for the effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section of our report, the aforesaid financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, or give a true and fair view in conformity with the applicable financial reporting framework. Reason: When issuing a qualified opinion due to a material misstatement (but not pervasive), the auditor should use the phrase: "except for the effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section of our report" This clearly limits the qualification to the specific issue. Options (b), (c), and (d) use incorrect or less appropriate wording. Hence, option (a) is the correct phrasing for the opinion paragraph.

Question 11. Which of the following is not correct: ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 573

(a) SA 700- Forming an Opinion and Reporting on Financial Statements (b) SA 705- Modified Opinion (c) SA 701- Communicating Key Audit Matters (d) SA 706-Comparative Information

(MTP Oct ‘20)

Ans: (d) SA 706-Comparative Information Reason: SA 706 deals with Emphasis of Matter Paragraphs and Other Matter Paragraphs, It does not deal with Comparative Information. Comparative information is covered under SA 710 - Comparative Information—Corresponding Figures and Comparative Financial Statements. Hence, option (d) is incorrect.

Question 12. Most of the auditor’s work in forming the auditor’s opinion consists of: (a) obtaining audit evidence. (b) evaluating audit evidence. (c) obtaining or evaluating audit evidence. (d) obtaining and evaluating audit evidence.

(MTP Oct 19, Apr 19)

Ans: (d) obtaining and evaluating audit evidence. Reason: Forming an auditor’s opinion requires both obtaining audit evidence and evaluating its sufficiency and appropriateness to draw conclusions. Both steps are essential and go hand-in-hand. Hence, option (d) is correct.

Question 13. Which of the following is correct: (a) The auditor shall express a qualified opinion when the auditor, having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, concludes that misstatements, individually or in the aggregate, are both material and pervasive to the financial statements. (b) The auditor shall express a disclaimer opinion when the auditor, having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, concludes that misstatements, individually or in the aggregate, are both material and pervasive to the financial statements. (c) The auditor shall express an adverse opinion when the auditor, having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, concludes that misstatements, individually or in the aggregate, are both material and pervasive to the financial statements. (d) The auditor shall express an adverse opinion when the auditor, having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, concludes that misstatements, individually or in the aggregate, are material, but not pervasive, to the financial statements

(MTP March ’19)

Ans: (c) The auditor shall express an adverse opinion when the auditor, having obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, concludes that misstatements, individually or in the aggregate, are both material and pervasive to the financial statements. ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 574

Reason: An adverse opinion is expressed when misstatements are both material and pervasive to the financial statements. A qualified opinion is for material but not pervasive misstatements. A disclaimer is when the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. Hence, option (c) is correct.

Question 14. An Audit report is: (a) An opinion drawn on the entity’s financial statements to make sure that the records are true and correct representation of the transactions they claim to represent. (b) An opinion drawn on the entity’s books of accounts to make sure that the records are true and fair representation of the transactions they claim to represent. (c) An opinion drawn on the entity’s financial statements to make sure that the records are true and fair representation of the transactions they claim to represent. (d) An opinion drawn on the entity’s books of accounts to make sure that the records are true and correct representation of the transactions they claim to represent.

(MTP Oct 19)

Ans: (c) An opinion drawn on the entity’s financial statements to make sure that the records are true and fair representation of the transactions they claim to represent. Reason: An audit report expresses an opinion on the financial statements (not just books of accounts) to confirm whether they give a true and fair view of the company’s financial position and transactions. The phrase “true and fair” is standard for audit opinions on financial statements. Options mentioning “books of accounts” or just “true and correct” are incomplete or inaccurate. Hence, option (c) is correct.

Question15. Which of following is not an element of audit report in accordance with SA 700? (a) Title (b) Addressee (c) Audit strategy (d) Auditor’s opinion

(MTP Oct ’23)

Ans: (c) Audit strategy Reason: The elements of an audit report under SA 700 include:  Title  Addressee  Auditor’s opinion  Basis for opinion  Management’s responsibility  Auditor’s responsibility  Other information, etc. Audit strategy is part of the auditor’s planning process, not part of the audit report. Hence, option (c) is not an element of the audit report.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 575

Question 16. An auditor disclaims opinion when\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_? (a) He is unable to obtain audit evidence and concludes that possible effects on financial statements of undetected misstatements could be material. (b) He is unable to obtain audit evidence and concludes that possible effects on financial statements of undetected misstatements could be both material and adverse. (c) He is unable to obtain audit evidence and concludes that possible effects on financial statements of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive. (d) He is unable to obtain audit evidence and concludes that possible effects on financial statements of undetected misstatements could be both material and perverse.

(MTP Oct ’23)

Ans: (c) (c) He is unable to obtain audit evidence and concludes that possible effects on financial statements of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive. Reason: An auditor disclaims an opinion when they cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence and believe that the possible effects on the financial statements could be both material and pervasive. “Pervasive” means affecting multiple areas or the financial statements as a whole. Options (a) and (b) do not specify “pervasive.” Option (d) contains a typo (“perverse” instead of “pervasive”). Hence, option (c) is correct.

Question 17. A company did not disclose accounting policies required to be disclosed under Schedule III or any other provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, the auditor should issue– (a) A qualified opinion (b) An adverse opinion (c) A disclaimer of opinion (d) Emphasis of matter paragraph.

(MTP Oct 19)

Ans: (a) A qualified opinion Reason: Non-disclosure of required accounting policies is a material misstatement but usually not pervasive. Hence, the auditor issues a qualified opinion for such a deficiency. An adverse opinion is reserved for material and pervasive misstatements. A disclaimer is for inability to obtain sufficient evidence. Emphasis of Matter is for matters appropriately disclosed, not omissions. So, option (a) is correct

Question 18. If the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the opening balances, (a) The auditor shall express a qualified opinion in accordance with SA 705. (b) The auditor shall express a disclaimer of opinion in accordance with SA 705. (c) The auditor shall express a qualified opinion or adverse opinion, as appropriate, in accordance with SA 705. (d) The auditor shall express a qualified opinion or a disclaimer of opinion, as appropriate, in accordance with SA 705\. ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 576

(MTP Oct 19, Apr’19 May’20, RTP Nov’19)

Ans: (d) The auditor shall express a qualified opinion or a disclaimer of opinion, as appropriate, in accordance with SA 705. Reason: If the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about opening balances, the auditor may either: Qualify the opinion if the possible effects are material but not pervasive, Or disclaim the opinion if the possible effects are material and pervasive. This guidance is in line with SA 705. Hence, option (d) is correct.

Question 19. Which of the following is incorrect: (a) Communicating key audit matters in the auditor’s report is not a substitute for disclosures in the financial statements that the applicable financial reporting framework requires management to make, or that are otherwise necessary to achieve fair presentation; (b) Communicating key audit matters in the auditor’s report is not a substitute for the auditor expressing a modified opinion when required by the circumstances of a specific audit engagement in accordance with SA 705 (Revised); (c) Communicating key audit matters in the auditor’s report is not a substitute for reporting in accordance with SA 570 when a material uncertainty exists relating to events or conditions that may cast significant doubt on an entity’s ability to continue as a going concern; (d) Communicating key audit matters in the auditor’s report is a substitute for the auditor expressing a modified opinion when required by the circumstances of a specific audit engagement in accordance with SA 705 (Revised);

(MTP April ’19)

Ans: (d) Communicating key audit matters in the auditor’s report is a substitute for the auditor expressing a modified opinion when required by the circumstances of a specific audit engagement in accordance with SA 705 (Revised)

Question 20. UDIN (Unique Document Identification Number) is required to be stated by practising Chartered Accountant on: - (a) Each audit report only (b) Each audit report and each certificate (c) Each audit report issued under Companies Act, 2013 only (d) Each audit report issued under Companies Act, 2013 only and each certificate

(MTP Oct ’23)

Ans: (b) Each audit report and each certificate Reason: As per ICAI guidelines, UDIN must be generated and mentioned on all audit reports as well as all certificates issued by a practicing Chartered Accountant. Hence, option (b) is correct

Question 21. Which of the following is not a duty of auditor to report under section 143 (1)

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 577

(a) whether loans and advances made by the company on the basis of security have been properly secured and whether the terms on which they have been made are prejudicial to the interests of the company or its members; (b) whether transactions of the company which are represented merely by book entries are prejudicial to the interests of the company; (c) where the company not being an investment company or a banking company, whether so much of the assets of the company as consist of shares, debentures and other securities have been sold at a price less than that at which they were purchased by the company; (d) whether the report on the accounts of any branch office of the company audited under sub-section (8) by a person other than the company’s auditors has been sent to him under the proviso to that sub-section and the manner in which he has dealt with it in preparing his report;

(MTP Oct’19)

Ans: (d) whether the report on the accounts of any branch office of the company audited under sub-section (8) by a person other than the company’s auditors has been sent to him under the proviso to that sub-section and the manner in which he has dealt with it in preparing his report; Reason: Section 143(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires auditors to report on loans, advances, book entry transactions, and asset sales. However, it does not require the auditor to report on how branch office audits (done by other auditors) are handled. That duty is specified under Section 143(8), not 143(1).

Question 22. Which of the following is correct as per section 143(10) of the Companies Act, 2013: (a) IFAC may prescribe the standards of auditing as recommended by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, in consultation with and after examination of the recommendations made by the National Financial Reporting Authority. (b) The International Auditing Standards Board may prescribe the standards of auditing as recommended by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, in consultation with and after examination of the recommendations made by the National Financial Reporting Authority. (c) The MCA may prescribe the standards of auditing as recommended by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, in consultation with and after examination of the recommendations made by the National Financial Reporting Authority. (d) The Central Government may prescribe the standards of auditing as recommended by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, in consultation with and after examination of the recommendations made by the National Financial Reporting Authority.

(MTP Oct’19)

Ans: (d) The Central Government may prescribe the standards of auditing as recommended by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, in consultation with and after examination of the recommendations made by the National Financial Reporting Authority. Reason: As per Section 143(10) of the Companies Act, 2013: The Central Government is empowered to prescribe the auditing standards, Based on recommendations by ICAI, In consultation with and after examining the recommendations of NFRA. Hence, option (d) is correct.

Question 23 Which of the following is FALSE regarding UDIN? (Unique document identification number) ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 578

(a) It is to be generated on UDIN portal. (b) Its basic objective is to help ICAI in keeping and maintaining an online registry of different services provided by all of its members. (c) It has to be generated and stated for each audit report signed by a Chartered Accountant. (d) It has to be generated and stated for each certificate signed by a Chartered Accountant.

(MTP Oct’22)

Ans: (b) Its basic objective is to help ICAI in keeping and maintaining an online registry of different services provided by all of its members. Reason: The primary objective of UDIN is to prevent forgery or misuse of Chartered Accountants’ signatures and to ensure authenticity of documents issued by them — not merely to maintain a registry of services. Hence, option (b) is false and therefore the correct answer.

Question 24 CASE STUDY M/s AB & Company is a firm of Chartered Accountants based in Mumbai. Mr. A and Mr. B are the Partners of the Firm. The Firm is engaged in various assignments including Audits. The partners are taking a summary of their work in order to prepare themselves to finalize the Audit and issue the audit report to various clients. You are requested to go through the following and answer the questions that follow:

- During the audit of M/s Persistent & Co, Mr. A found that the firm has changed the method of Depreciation

from WDV to SLM but has not given the retrospective effect. Mr. A has calculated the difference of depreciation but M/s Persistent & Co. has stated that they don’t want to change the financial statements and if auditor persists they may give the effect in the next financial year.

- During the audit of M/s Dubious Brothers, Mr B observed that the firm had a very large amount of cash sales

and there were no details of the customers to whom the sales were made. Further, cash generated was not even deposited into bank regularly. When Mr. B asked the firm to give him an opportunity to count cash, the manager of the firm said that the cash is with the owner and it cannot be made available to the auditor for the checking purpose. The manager also declined to give an opportunity for stock verification to Mr B.

- During the audit of M/s Honest & Associates, Mr. A came to know that the firm has changed its method of

valuation of stock. This change has a material impact on the financial statement of the firm. The firm has made relevant disclosures in the financial statements and has given proper accounting treatment to this exercise. (Study material) MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS (MCQS) Based on above, answer the following questions: -

1. In case of M/s Persistent & Company, what would be an ideal Audit Opinion?

(a) Unmodified (b) Qualified (c) Mention the fact in Emphasis of Matter Paragraph (d) Disclaimer

Ans: (b) Qualified Reason: In the case of M/s Persistent & Company, a qualified opinion is appropriate when: The auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, But concludes that misstatements are material, yet not pervasive to the financial statements. ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 579

This usually happens when there's an identified issue, such as: Non-compliance with accounting standards, Incorrect presentation or disclosure, or Valuation errors , that do not affect the overall financial statements to a pervasive extent. Hence, a "Qualified Opinion" is ideal when the misstatement is material but not pervasive — matching the situation in Persistent & Company as described in the ICAI study material.

2. In case of M/s Dubious Brothers, what Audit Opinion should the Auditor give?

(a) Qualified (b) Adverse (c) Disclaimer (d) Unmodified

Ans: (c) Disclaimer Reason (as per ICAI study material): In the case of M/s Dubious Brothers, the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, and the possible effects of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive. As per SA 705 (Revised), when the auditor: I. Cannot obtain audit evidence, and II. Believes the impact could be material and pervasive, the correct opinion is a Disclaimer of Opinion. Thus, option (c) is correct — the auditor should issue a Disclaimer, as per the ICAI study material.

3. According to you, what would be appropriate course to take in case of M/s Honest & Associates?

(a) Issue Qualified Opinion (b) Issue Adverse Opinion (c) Mention the fact of change in method in Emphasis of Matter Paragraph (d) Issue Disclaimer of Opinion

Ans: (c) Mention the fact of change in method in Emphasis of Matter Paragraph Reason: When there is a change in accounting method that is properly disclosed and acceptable, it does not affect the overall fairness of the financial statements, so an Emphasis of Matter paragraph is sufficient to highlight the change to users.

4. When the Auditor, after conclusion of an Audit exercise, is of the opinion that there are material

misstatements in the Financial Statements, but they are not pervasive, then what should an Auditor do? (a) Issue Unmodified Opinion (b) Issue Qualified Opinion (c) Issue Disclaimer of Opinion (d) Mention it in Emphasis of Matter Paragraph

Ans: (b) Issue Qualified Opinion

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 580

Reason: When material misstatements exist but are not pervasive, the auditor issues a Qualified Opinion to highlight the specific issues while confirming that the rest of the financial statements are fairly presented.

5. When the Auditor concludes that the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in

accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework, Auditor shall give: (a) Modified Opinion (b) Qualified Opinion (c) Disclaimer of Opinion (d) Unmodified Opinion

Ans: (d) Unmodified Opinion Reason: When financial statements are free from material misstatements and comply with the applicable framework, the auditor issues an Unmodified Opinion, indicating a clean and fair presentation.

Question 25. While expressing an unmodified opinion on financial statements, the auditor shall not use which of the following phrases? (a) present fairly in all material respects (b) give a true and fair view (c) with the foregoing explanation (d) All of the above

(Study material)

Ans: (c) with the foregoing explanation Reason: The phrase "with the foregoing explanation" suggests a reservation or qualification, which is inconsistent with an unmodified (clean) opinion.

Question 26. …………………… is a paragraph included in the auditor’s report that refers to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements that, in the auditor’s judgement, is of such importance that it is fundamental to the user’s understanding of the financial statements. (a) Emphasis of Matter Paragraph (b) Other Matter Paragraph (c) Key Audit Matter (d) Management Responsibility Paragraph.

(Study material)

Ans: (a) Emphasis of Matter Paragraph Reason: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph highlights important disclosures already in the financial statements that are crucial for users’ understanding without modifying the auditor’s opinion.

Question 27. Statement 1: Communicating key audit matter in the auditor’s report constitutes a substitute for disclosure in the financial statements. Statement 2: Instead of modifying an opinion in accordance with SA 705, the statutory auditor can use Key Audit Matter paragraph in the audit report with an unmodified opinion. (a) Only Statement 1 is correct ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 581

(b) Only Statement 2 is correct (c) Both the statements are correct (d) None of the statement is correct

(Study material)

Ans: (d) None of the statement is correct Reason: Key Audit Matters are communicated in addition to, not as a substitute for, disclosures in the financial statements. Also, they do not replace the need to modify an opinion when required under SA 705

Question 28. Which of the following is not correct? (a) SA 700 - Forming an Opinion and Reporting on the Financial Statements (b) SA 701- Key Audit Matters in the Independent Auditor’s Report (c) SA 705- Comparative Information- Corresponding figures and Comparative Financial Statements (d) SA 706- Emphasis of Matter Paragraphs and Other Matter Paragraphs in the Independent Auditor’s Report

(Study material)

Ans: (c) SA 705- Comparative Information- Corresponding figures and Comparative Financial Statements Reason: SA 705 deals with Modifications to the Opinion in the Independent Auditor’s Report, not comparative information. Comparative information is covered under a different standard, SA 710.

Question 29. Responsibilities of Joint Auditors are governed by: (a) SA 200 (b) SA 229 (c) SA 299 (d) SA 230

(Study material)

Ans: (c) SA 299 Reason: SA 299 specifically deals with the responsibilities of joint auditors, outlining how they should cooperate and coordinate during the audit.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 582

Chapter 9 AUDIT OF DIFFERENT TYPES OF ENTITIES

Question 1. It is the duty of Comptroller and Auditor General of India to audit and report on all expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India and of each State and of each Union Territory having a Legislative Assembly and to ascertain whether the moneys shown in the accounts as having been disbursed were legally available for and applicable to the service or purpose to which they have been applied or charged and whether the expenditure conforms to the authority which governs it. Discuss, in above context, what is understood by “Consolidated Fund of India”? What is its importance?

(2 Marks|3 Minutes)(Study material)(Easy)

Answer 1. Consolidated Fund of India consists of all the revenue received from direct and indirect taxes, all the loans taken by the Govt. of India and all the amount of repayment of loans received by the Govt. of India. Its importance lies in the fact that all government expenditure is incurred from this fund. No moneys out of the Consolidated Fund of India shall be appropriated except in accordance with law and for the purposes and in the manner provided in the Constitution.

Approach & time saving tips Approach : Define Consolidated Fund of India first, then mention its components and constitutional importance. Link it with government expenditure control. Time Saving Tips: Write definition in one line and directly state “all government expenditure is incurred from this fund.” Avoid lengthy constitutional explanation.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Students often forget to mention loans and loan recoveries as part of the fund. Many also ignore “appropriation by law” point.

Question 2. CA Akash Virmani is auditor of a partnership firm consisting of 4 partners. During the year, one of the partners has retired and another partner has joined the next day. Discuss, any one point, which shall be considered by you to ensure that financial statements of firm are not misstated due to change of constitution of firm.

(2 Marks|3 Minutes)(Study material (Easy)

Answer 2. The auditor shall consider provisions of retirement deed/partnership deed for date of retiring and joining of partners. It should be ensured that profits are appropriately distributed up to date of retirement. Further, profits after retirement should have been distributed among partners as per terms of new partnership deed.

Approach & time saving tips Approach : Focus on effect of change in constitution of partnership and profit sharing before and after retirement/admission. Time Saving Tips: Mention retirement deed/new partnership deed directly instead of writing general audit procedures.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 583

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Students commonly forget date-wise allocation of profit and impact on financial statements.

Question 3. You are appointed as an auditor of M/s Shine & Co., a partnership firm. During your review, you observed that:

- The audit appointment was informal and not documented properly.
- The firm started a new business activity which is not covered in the partnership deed.
- Major financial decisions were made without proper records.

As an auditor, briefly explain the matters that should be specially considered by you while auditing the accounts of the partnership firm, M/s Shine & Co.

(6 Marks|5-6 Minutes) (RTP Sept 2025)(Medium)

Answer 3. While auditing the accounts of M/s Shine & Co., a partnership firm, it is important to ensure that they have formal appointment. Further, deviation from the partnership deed, and absence of documentation for key decisions raise concerns about the validity, transparency, and legal compliance of the firm’s operations. Thus, the auditor should specially consider the following matters in the audit of accounts of a partnership: (i) Letter of Appointment: Confirming that the letter of appointment, signed by a partner, duly authorised, clearly states the nature and scope of audit contemplated by the partners, specially the limitation, if any, under which the auditor shall have to function. (ii) Partnership Documents: Studying the minute book, if any, maintained to record the policy decision taken by partners specially the minutes relating to authorisation of extraordinary and capital expenditure, raising of loans; purchase of assets, extraordinary contracts entered into and other such matters as are not of a routine nature. (iii) Objects of Partnership: Verifying that the business in which the partnership is engaged is authorised by the partnership agreement; or by any extension or modification thereof agreed to subsequently. (iv) Books of Account: Examining whether books of account appear to be reasonable and are considered adequate in relation to the nature of the business of the partnership. (v) Mutual Interest: Verifying generally that the interest of no partner has suffered prejudicially by an activity engaged in by the partnership which, it was not authorised to do under the partnership deed or by any violation of a provision in the partnership agreements. (vi) Provision for Taxes: Confirming that a provision for the firm’s tax payable by the partnership has been made in the accounts before arriving at the amount of profit divisible among the partners. (vii) Division of Profits: Verifying that the profits and losses have been divided among the partners in their agreed profit-sharing ratio. (1+5 Marks)

Approach & time saving tips Approach : Divide answer into separate audit considerations like appointment, partnership deed, books, profits, taxes etc. Time Saving Tips: Use headings and keywords from study material; avoid detailed explanations for each point.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Many students write only partnership deed points and ignore books of account, tax provision and mutual interest verification.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 584

Question 4. You are auditor of a school operating in your city. During audit of a year, it is noticed that fees concessions to students have been provided in substantial number of cases. Discuss, how, you as an auditor, would proceed to verify the same?

(2 marks|3 Minutes) (Study material)(Easy)

Answer 4. The fees concessions have to be under proper authority of school management. The auditor would verify internal controls in this regard. Besides, detailed checking of few cases needs to be undertaken to ensure genuineness of fees concessions and proper management approvals.

Approach & time saving tips Approach : Explain verification of fee concessions with authority approval and test checking of cases. Time Saving Tips: Write “verify management approval + detailed checking of selected cases.” Keep answer concise.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Students generally miss internal control verification regarding concessions.

Question 5. A society has been formed by pan India employees of a public sector bank. The purpose of society is to promote savings habits of members and to grant loan to them up to a small specified amount. Small savings are promoted amongst members by way of compulsory contribution from monthly salary. Identify type of society and also discuss nature of books of accounts to be maintained by such a society.

(2 Marks|3 Minutes) (Study material)(Easy)

Answer 5. The society is in nature of Multi-state cooperative society as it serves interests of members in more than one state. It accepts small savings from its members and grants loan to members. As per Multi-State Co- operative Society Rules 2002, every Multi- State Co-operative society shall keep books of account with respect to: (a) all sum of money received and expended and matters in respect of which the receipt and expenditure take place (b) the assets and liabilities

Approach & time saving tips Approach : Identify type of society first, then state books of account required under Multi-State Co-operative Society Rules. Time Saving Tips: Use direct points instead of explaining society features repeatedly.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Students often fail to identify it as a Multi-State Co-operative Society.

Question 6. What is the significance of the Consolidated Fund of India in the context of government auditing, and how does it relate to the role of the Public Accounts Committee?

(4 Marks|6 Minutes) (Study material)(Easy)

Answer 6. Introduction: The Consolidated Fund of India is a critical component of government financial management, serving as the primary account for all government revenues and expenditures. Government

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 585

auditing ensures accountability in managing this fund, and the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) plays a vital role in this process. Parts:  The Consolidated Fund of India includes all revenues (taxes, loans, and repayments) and is the source from which government expenditures are made, as approved by Parliament through demands for grants.  Government auditing verifies that funds from the Consolidated Fund are used as per parliamentary approvals, ensuring transparency and accountability.  The PAC examines the Appropriation Accounts, which detail actual expenditures against budgeted allocations, to ensure compliance and detect any mismanagement or irregularities.  Through its scrutiny, the PAC ensures that the executive is held accountable for the proper utilization of public funds, aligning with the objectives of government auditing. Conclusion: The Consolidated Fund of India is central to government financial operations, and it’s auditing, supported by the PAC’s oversight, ensures fiscal discipline and accountability in public expenditure.

Approach & time saving tips Approach : Explain link between Consolidated Fund, government audit and PAC in sequence. Time Saving Tips: Use introduction–points–conclusion format with short bullet points.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Students usually explain only the fund and forget PAC’s role in accountability.

Question 7. The C&AG compiles the annual accounts for a State, including receipts and disbursements, based on data from state treasuries. The submission deadline is agreed upon with the Governor. However, due to delays in receiving treasury data, the C&AG submits the accounts after the deadline, prompting the State Government to question the validity of the report. Is the delayed submission compliant with the C&AG’s duties?

(5 Marks|7 Minutes) (RTP May 2022)(Medium)

Answer 7. Reference: Section 10 of the Comptroller & Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 describe provisions related to this situation. Provision Applicable: The C&AG is responsible for compiling accounts of the Union and each State from initial and subsidiary accounts provided by treasuries, offices, or departments. The C&AG prepares annual statements of receipts and disbursements and submits them to the President, Governor, or Administrator by a specified date determined in consultation with the concerned government. Facts of the Case: The C&AG compiled the State’s annual accounts using treasury data but submitted the accounts to the Governor after the agreed deadline due to delays in receiving data from state treasuries. The State Government questions the validity of the delayed report. Related Facts of the Case with Provision and Analysis: Section 10 of the 1971 Act mandates the C&AG to compile and submit accounts by a deadline set in consultation with the government. However, the Act does not specify penalties for delays caused by external factors, such as late submission of data by treasuries. The C&AG’s duty is to ensure accuracy and completeness, which may be compromised if rushed due to external delays. The delay does not invalidate the report if it meets the standards of accuracy and completeness, but the C&AG must coordinate with the State to prevent future delays, as the deadline is set collaboratively.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 586

Reason: The delay was due to external factors (late treasury data), and the Act does not deem delayed submissions invalid, provided the accounts are accurate and complete. Conclusion with Short Reason and Reference Again: The delayed submission is compliant, as the Act prioritizes accuracy over strict adherence to deadlines caused by external delays. Reference: Section 10 of the Comptroller & Auditor General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971.

Approach & time saving tips Approach : Apply Section 10 provisions with facts and conclude whether delayed submission invalidates report. Time Saving Tips: Mention “accuracy and completeness prevail over procedural delay.”

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Many students wrongly conclude delay makes report invalid.

Question 8. The Public Works Department of a state government incurred an expenditure of ₹ 75 lakhs on constructing a community hall without obtaining approval through competitive bidding as mandated by the General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017. The department justified the expenditure citing urgency due to an upcoming election. As a statutory auditor, evaluate the compliance of this expenditure with the relevant audit standards.

(4 Marks|6 Minutes)(Study material)(Medium)

Answer 8. Reference: This question is related to the Comptroller and Auditor General's (CAG) Manual of Standing Orders (Audit), Section on Audit against Rules & Orders. Provision Applicable: Audit against Rules & Orders ensures government expenditure aligns with constitutional provisions, laws, and financial regulations, including General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017. Rule 154 of GFR mandates competitive bidding for procurements above Rs. 25,000 to ensure transparency and economy. Article 166 of the Constitution requires executive actions to comply with established rules. Facts of the Case: The Public Works Department spent ₹ 75 lakhs on a community hall without competitive bidding, claiming urgency due to an election. No documented evidence supported the urgency, and the expenditure was approved by the department head without following GFR procedures. Related Facts of the Case with Provision and Analysis: GFR Rule 154 requires e-procurement or competitive bidding to ensure cost-effectiveness and transparency. The department’s claim of urgency lacks substantiation, as no emergency clause was invoked under GFR Rule 166 (exception for urgency). Analysis reveals that similar projects in other districts followed bidding, securing lower costs. The expenditure violates Article 166, as it bypasses mandatory financial rules, risking overpricing or favouritism. Reason: Non-compliance with GFR 2017 and lack of documented justification for bypassing bidding indicate a violation of financial regulations and constitutional safeguards. Conclusion with Short Reason and Reference Again: The expenditure is irregular due to non-adherence to competitive bidding requirements, necessitating recovery or regularization as per Comptroller and Auditor General's (CAG) Manual of Standing Orders (Audit), Section on Audit against Rules & Orders.

Approach & time saving tips Approach : Identify violation of GFR competitive bidding rules and connect with audit against rules and orders. Time Saving Tips: Quote Rule 154 briefly and conclude expenditure is irregular.

Examiner observation

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 587

Examiner Observation : Students forget to analyse urgency exception and documentation requirement.

Question 9. A state government’s sanitation program aimed to construct 1,000 public toilets with a ₹ 50 crore budget. Only 600 toilets were built, costing ₹ 60 crores due to inefficient contractor selection and poor resource management. As a statutory auditor, evaluate the program’s performance in terms of efficiency, economy, and effectiveness.

(4 Marks|6 Minutes)(MTP Nov 2020)(Medium)

Answer 9. Reference: CAG's Performance Auditing Guidelines, 2014 deals with this type of situation. Provision Applicable: Performance audit evaluates efficiency (economic execution yielding results), economy (cost-effective resource use), and effectiveness (achieving objectives efficiently). It involves steps like topic identification, planning, execution, and reporting to identify opportunities for improved economy and effectiveness. Facts of the Case: The sanitation program targeted 1,000 toilets with a ₹ 50 crore budget but delivered only 600 toilets at ₹ 60 crores due to inefficient contractor selection and underutilized resources. Related Facts of the Case with Provision and Analysis: Performance audit requires assessing if resources were used economically and objectives met effectively. The program failed in effectiveness (600 vs. 1,000 toilets), economy (overspent by ₹ 10 crores), and efficiency (poor contractor management). Analysis shows similar programs in other states achieved 90% targets at lower costs. Related facts indicate inadequate planning and monitoring, as per CAG guidelines. Reason: The program’s failure in meeting targets, cost overruns, and inefficient resource use indicate poor performance across audit parameters. Conclusion with Short Reason and Reference Again: The program is inefficient, uneconomical, and ineffective, requiring corrective measures for future projects. Reference: CAG's Performance Auditing Guidelines, 2014.

Approach & time saving tips Approach : Evaluate separately under economy, efficiency and effectiveness. Time Saving Tips: Make a 3-column style mental structure for quick presentation.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Students mix up efficiency and effectiveness concepts.

Question 10. The Commercial Tax Department of a state government collected ₹ 100 crores as Goods and Services Tax from businesses in a financial year. During the audit, it was found that ₹ 5 crores was incorrectly assessed due to misclassification of taxable goods. As a statutory auditor, evaluate the compliance of this receipt with audit standards.

(4 Marks|6 Minutes) (Study Material)(Medium)

Answer 10. Reference: CAG Manual of Standing Orders (Audit), Section on Audit of Receipts deals with this type of situation. Provision Applicable: The audit of receipts involves verifying the correct assessment, realization, and crediting of government revenues by designated authorities. It ensures compliance with relevant tax laws (e.g., CGST Act,

2017. and checks for errors, omissions, or fraud in the assessment process, as per the CAG’s guidelines.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 588

Facts of the Case: The Commercial Tax Department collected ₹ 100 crores in GST, but ₹ 5 crores was incorrectly assessed due to misclassification of taxable goods under a lower tax slab, leading to under-collection of revenue. Related Facts of the Case with Provision and Analysis: The CGST Act, 2017, mandates accurate classification of goods for GST assessment. The audit provision requires verifying correct assessment to prevent revenue loss. Analysis reveals that the department failed to implement proper checks for classification, violating Section 9 of the CGST Act. Reason: The incorrect assessment due to misclassification resulted in revenue loss, indicating a failure in the department’s internal controls and audit checks. Conclusion with Short Reason and Reference Again: The receipt is irregular due to incorrect assessment, necessitating recovery of the under-assessed amount and improved controls. Reference: CAG's Manual of Standing Orders (Audit), Section on Audit of Receipts.

Approach & time saving tips Approach : Explain audit of receipts and relate incorrect GST classification with revenue loss. Time Saving Tips: Directly connect misclassification with under-assessment and weak internal controls.
