Question 61. Lifeline Hospital, a charitable healthcare institution, provides medical services at subsidised rates. During the audit for the financial year 2024– to some patients even though they were

government health scheme were recorded, but supporting documentation or correspondenc The hospital maintained a large stock of medicines and medical supplies, however, there were no proper

expenditures, particularly in staff salaries and equipment maintenance, but no explanation was documented by the management. In view of above, discuss the special step or audit procedures an auditor should apply while auditing the transactions of hospital?

(5 marks|7 Minutes)[Easy|ICAI Fav]

Answer: The special step or audit procedures an auditor should apply while auditing the transactions of hospital are: (i) Register of Patients: Vouch the Register of patients with copies of bills issued to them. Verify bills for a selected period with the patients’ attendance record to see that the bills have been correctly prepared. Also see that bills have been issued to all patients from whom an amount was recoverable according to the rules of the hospital.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 621

(ii) Collection of Cash: Check cash collections as entered in the Cash Book with the receipts, counterfoils and other evidence for example, copies of patients bills, counterfoils of dividend and other interest warrants, copies of rent bills, etc. (iii) Income from Investments, Rent etc: See with reference to the property and Investment Register that all income that should have been received by way of rent on properties, dividends, and interest on securities have been collected. (iv) Legacies and Donations: Ascertain that legacies and donations received for a specific purpose have been applied in the manner agreed upon. (v) Reconciliation of Subscriptions: Trace all collections of subscription and donations from the Cash Book to the respective Registers. Reconcile the total subscriptions due (as shown by the Subscription Register and the amount collected and that still outstanding). (vi) Authorisation and Sanctions: Vouch all purchases and expenses and verify that the capital expenditure was incurred only with the prior sanction of the Trustees or the Managing Committee and that appointments and increments to staff have been duly authorised. (vii) Grants and TDS: Verify that grants, if any, received from Government or local authority has been duly accounted for. Also, that refund in respect of taxes deducted at source has been claimed. (viii) Budgets: Compare the totals of various items of expenditure and income with the amount budgeted for them and report to the Trustees or the Managing Committee, significant variations which have taken place. (ix) Internal Check: Examine the internal check as regards the receipt and issue of stores; medicines, linen, apparatus, clothing, instruments, etc. so as to ensure that purchases have been properly recorded in the Inventory Register and that issues have been made only against proper authorisation. (x) Depreciation: See that depreciation has been written off against all the assets at the appropriate rates. (xi) Registers: Inspect the bonds, share scrips, title deeds of properties and compare their particulars with those entered in the property and Investment Registers. (xii) Inventories: Obtain inventories, especially of stocks and stores as at the end of the year and check a percentage of the items physically; also compare their total values with respective ledger balances. (xiii) Management Representation and Certificate: Get proper Management Representation and Certificate with respect to various aspects covered during the course of audit.

Time saving tips & approach Approach : Correlate each defect with the audit procedure: Patients ↔ Bills, Donations ↔ Specific purpose, Grants ↔ Documentation, Stores ↔ Internal control, Time Saving Tips: Remember Patient → Cash → Donations → Grants → Budget → Stores → Assets. Focus on issues specifically highlighted in the question. Write short audit procedures rather than lengthy explanations.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Students often miss specific-purpose donations. Weak answers ignore inventory/stores controls. Budget comparison and reporting of significant variances is frequently omitted.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 622

Question 62. Serving Fingers Foundation, a registered NGO based in Delhi, launched a nationwide donation drive during the year 2024–25 to support victims of a flood in Assam. The NGO received substantial donations from individuals, corporates, and international donors. These funds were then sent to to different NGOs operating in Assam, who were actively involved in flood relief work. Serving Fingers Foundation has appointed you to audit its accounts for the year in which it collected and remitted donations for flood victims. Draft audit programme for audit of receipts of donations and remittance of the collected amount to different NGOs. Mention three points each, peculiar to the situation, which you will like to incorporate in your audit programme for audit of said receipts and remittances of donations.

(5 marks|7 Minutes)[Moderate|ICAI Fav]

Answer. In the given situation, the audit programme should include the following specific points for audit of receipts and remittances of donation. Receipt of Donations: (i) Internal Control System: Existence of internal control system particularly with reference to division of responsibilities in respect of authorised collection of donations, custody of receipt books and safe custody of money. (ii) Custody of Receipt Books: Existence of system regarding issue of receipt books, whether unused receipt books are returned and the same are verified physically including checking of number of receipt books and sequence of numbering therein. (iii) Receipt of Cheques: Receipt Book should have carbon copy for duplicate receipt and signed by a responsible official. All details relating to date of cheque, bank’s name, date, amount, etc. should be clearly stated. (iv) Bank Reconciliation: Reconciliation of bank statements with reference to all cash deposits not only with reference to date and amount but also with reference to receipt book. (v) Cash Receipts: Register of cash donations to be vouched more extensively. If addresses are available of donors who had given cash, the same may be cross-checked by asking entity to post thank you letters mentioning amount, date and receipt number. (vi) Foreign Contributions, if any, to receive special attention to compliance with applicable laws and regulations. Remittance of Donations to Different NGOs: (i) Mode of Sending Remittance: All remittances are through account payee cheques. Remittances through Demand Draft would also need to be scrutinised thoroughly with reference to recipient. (ii) Confirming Receipt of Remittance: All remittances are supported by receipts and acknowledgements. (iii) Identity: Recipient NGO is a genuine entity. Verify address, 80G Registration Number, etc. (iv) Direct Confirmation Procedure: Send confirmation letters to entities to whom donations have been paid. (v) Donation Utilisation: Utilisation of donations for providing relief to Tsunami victims and not for any other purpose. (vi) System of NGOs’ Selection: System for selecting NGO to whom donations have been sent.

Time saving tips & approach Approach : For receipts: Internal controls, receipt books, bank reconciliation. For remittances: Recipient verification, acknowledgements, utilisation of funds. Mention foreign contribution compliance if donations include overseas donors. Time Saving Tips: Divide answer into Receipts (3 points) and Remittances (3 points). Use separate headings to score presentation marks. Focus on controls, documentation and confirmation.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 623

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Students write generic NGO audit points instead of donation-specific points. Identity verification of recipient NGOs is commonly missed. Utilisation of donations for intended purpose is an important scoring point

Question 63. ABC Ltd. is a government company whose statutory audit is being carried out by auditors appointed on the advice of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (C&AG). During the audit, the C&AG considered it necessary to conduct a test audit of the company’s accounts. He issued specific directions to the statutory auditors regarding the system of book-keeping and internal control. After completion of the statutory audit, the auditors submitted a copy of their report to the C&AG, who added certain comments and supplementary observations to it. The Board of Directors of ABC Ltd., however, decided not to provide any explanation or reply to the comments made by the C&AG. Based on above, explain the powers of the C&AG in relation to the test audit of a government company and whether the Board of Directors is required to provide any explanation on the C&AG’s comments.

(4 marks|6 Minutes)[Moderate|ICAI Fav]

Answer: 1) Without prejudice to the provisions relating to audit and auditor, the Comptroller and Auditor- General of India may, in case of any company covered under sub-section (5) or sub-section (7) of section 139, if he considers necessary, by an order, cause test audit to be conducted of the accounts of such company and the provisions of section 19A of the Comptroller and Auditor- General’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, shall apply to the report of such test audit.

2. The C&AG shall direct the manner in which the company’s accounts shall be audited by the statutory auditors

and give such auditors instructions in regard to any matter relating to the performance of his functions as such. The directions under section 143(6) broadly cover the system of book-keeping and accounts, internal control etc.

3. The C&AG has power to conduct a supplementary or test audit of the company’s accounts by such person as he

may authorise in this behalf and for the purposes of such audit require information or additional information to be furnished to any person or persons so authorised on such matters by such person or persons and in such form as the C&AG may by general or special order, direct.

4. The statutory auditors shall submit a copy of their audit report to C&AG who shall have a right to comment

upon or supplement the audit report submitted by the statutory auditors in such manner as he may think fit. Section 134(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 imposes a duty on the board of directors of a company to give an explanation or comments on every reservation, or adverse remarks or disclaimer contained in the auditors’ report and secretarial audit report of the Company Secretary in practice. In the absence of similar provisions requiring the company to give reply on the reservation made by the C&AG, the board of directors of such a company is not bound to give information or explanation in respect of such comments.

Time saving tips & approach Approach : First explain C&AG powers under Companies Act. Then explain statutory auditor's duty to submit report to C&AG. Finally conclude that Board is not legally bound to reply to C&AG comments. Time Saving Tips: Remember Directions → Test Audit → Supplementary Audit → Comments. Quote section-based powers briefly. Separate powers from Board's responsibility.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 624

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Students confuse statutory audit with test/supplementary audit. Many incorrectly state that Board must reply to C&AG comments. Mention that C&AG can issue directions regarding book-keeping and internal controls.

Question 64. Sun and Moon Credit Co-operative Society Ltd., a large scale cooperative organisation operates in Maharashtra and engages in providing small loans to its members. During the audit, the auditor observed that the society maintains a Cash Book and Ledger but has not maintained separate registers for loan disbursement and recovery of loans from members’ salaries. The management contends that since they maintain the main Cash Book, there is no need to maintain other subsidiary records. As an auditor, explain whether the society’s practice is appropriate and what records should be maintained.

(4 marks|6 Minutes)[Easy|ICAI Fav]

Answer. 1) In Maharashtra, the co-operative societies are required to maintain books of account in terms of the instructions of the Registrar as following: (i) All sums of money received and expended by the society and the matters in respect of which receipts and expenditure take place. (ii) All sales and purchases of goods by the society. (iii) Assets and liabilities of the society.

2. In order to maintain proper financial accounting records so as to disclose full financial results of working of the

society, the statutory or mandatory provisions provide a directive, but they are not conclusive. The society is at liberty to maintain such additional records according to its convenience and which it thinks more useful for clarity and detailed explanation. Ultimately the financial transactions and the results thereof must be presented very clearly and in the best possible manner.

3. Depending upon the nature and object of the society, different kinds of books and registers will be maintained,

so as to disclose a proper and fair picture of financial transactions. In case of large scale co-operative organisation, different subsidiary books and registers shall be maintained and the daily summary totals will be transferred to main Cash Book. For example: a) Daily cash sales summary register. b) A register of collection from debtors if credit sales are allowed by bye-laws of society. c) A register of recovery of loans from salaries and directly by receipts from members in case of credit society. d) Loan disbursement register in case of credit society. e) Any other columnar subsidiaries depending upon the nature and functions of society.

Time saving tips & approach Approach : State statutory requirements. Explain that large societies need subsidiary records. Specifically mention Loan Disbursement Register and Loan Recovery Register. Time Saving Tips: Remember Cash Book ≠ Sufficient. Mention mandatory books first and additional subsidiary registers later. Focus on loan-related records.

Examiner observation

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 625

Examiner Observation : Students merely list books without explaining the need for subsidiary records. Loan recovery register is frequently omitted. Examiner expects practical examples of additional registers.

Question 65. State the auditor's duty regarding audit of LLP.

(4 marks|6 Minutes)[Easy|ICAI Fav]

Answer: Auditor’s Duty Regarding Audit of LLP

1. Engagement Letter: The auditor should get definite instructions in writing as to the work to be performed by

him.

2. Minutes Book: If partners maintain minute book he shall refer it for any resolution passed regarding the

accounts

3. LLP Agreement: The auditor should read the LLP agreement & note the following provisions:

(i) Nature of the business of the LLP. (ii) Amount of capital contributed by each partner. (iii) Interest – in respect of additional capital contributed. (iv) Duration of partnership. (v) Drawings allowed to the partners. (vi) Salaries, commission etc. payable to partners. (vii) Borrowing powers of the LLP. (viii) Rights & duties of partners. (ix) Method of settlement of accounts between partners at the time of admission, retirement, admission etc. (x) Any loans advanced by the partners. (xi) Profit sharing ratio

4. Reporting: The auditor should mention:

(i) Whether the records of the firm appear to be correct & reliable. (ii) Whether he was able to obtain all information & explanation necessary for his work. (iii) Whether any restriction was imposed upon him.

Time saving tips & approach Approach : Begin with engagement instructions. Explain examination of LLP Agreement and important clauses. End with reporting responsibilities. Time Saving Tips: Remember Engagement Letter → Minutes → LLP Agreement → Reporting. LLP Agreement is the most important part of the answer. Write headings and sub-points.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Students write company audit duties instead of LLP-specific duties. Important LLP Agreement clauses such as capital contribution and profit-sharing ratio are often missed. Reporting requirements should be stated separately.

Question 66. XYZ Sewa Foundation a registered NGO receives income from various sources such as foreign grants, membership fees, subscription etc. As the audit assistant you are assigned to verify the receipt of

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 626

income of the NGO for the year. You are required to describe the audit procedures you would perform to verify the receipt of income of an NGO.

(4 marks|6 Minutes)[Easy|ICAI Fav]

Answer: The receipt of income of NGO may be checked o n the following lines: i) Contributions and Grants for projects and programmes: Check agreements with donors and grants letters to ensure that funds received have been accounted for. Check that all foreign contribution receipts are deposited in the foreign contribution bank account as notified under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 ii) Receipts from fund raising programmes: Verify in detail the internal control system and ascertain who are the persons responsible for collection of funds and mode of receipt. Ensure that collections are counted and deposited in the bank daily. iii) Membership Fees: Check fees received with Membership Register. Ensure proper classification is made between entrance and annual fees and life membership fees. Reconcile fees received with fees to be received during the year. iv) Subscriptions: Check with subscription register and receipts issued. Reconcile subscription received with printing and dispatch of corresponding magazine / circulars / periodicals. Check the receipts with subscription rate schedule. v) Interest and Dividends: Check the interest and dividends received and receivable with investments held during the year.

Time saving tips & approach Approach : Mention supporting documents for every income source. Reconcile registers with receipts and collections. Specifically mention compliance with FCRA for foreign contributions. Time Saving Tips: Remember Grants → Fund Raising → Membership → Subscription → Interest. Each source of income requires a separate verification procedure. Keep answer source-wise.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Students forget FCRA compliance. Membership fees and subscriptions are often mixed up. Reconciliation procedures are important for scoring full marks.

Question 66. In Audit against Rules & Orders of government expenditure audit, the executive government frames various rules, regulations and orders that are to be observed by sub-ordinate authorities. It is the function of audit to see that these rules, regulations and orders are applied properly by the sub-ordinate authorities. State the important points that an auditor must ensure while carrying out the examination of various rules, regulation and orders issued by the executive authorities.

(4 marks|6 Minutes)[Easy|ICAI Fav]

Answer: While carrying out the examination of the various rules, regulations and orders issued by the executive authorities, the auditor must ensure that: i) They are not inconsistent with any provisions of the Constitution, or any laws made thereunder; ii) They are consistent with the essential requirements of audit and accounts as determined by the C\&AG; iii) They do not come in conflict with the orders of, or rules made by, any higher authority; and ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 627

iv) In case they have not been separately approved by competent authority, the issuing authority possesses the necessary rule-making power.

Time saving tips & approach Approach : Start with "Auditor should ensure that..." Present all four points in bullet form. Use keywords exactly as given in the standard answer. Time Saving Tips: Remember Constitution → C&AG → Higher Authority → Rule-making Power. Only four points; write them exactly. This is a direct memory-based question.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Students write general audit procedures instead of conditions for examination of rules. Missing any one of the four conditions generally results in loss of marks. Use precise language such as not inconsistent, not in conflict, necessary rule-making power.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 628

### (Multiple Choices Questins )MCQ

MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS (MCQS) Question 1. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the evolution of government audit in India post-independence? a) Government audit initially focused solely on expenditure but later expanded to include receipts and commercial audits. b) The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) is responsible for auditing government revenue and expenditure before the funds are disbursed. c) Government audit has adapted general auditing principles while introducing new concepts for governmental transactions. d) The scope of government audit now includes auditing non-commercial autonomous bodies for public accountability.

(MTP Oct 2021)

Ans: b) The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) is responsible for auditing government revenue and expenditure before the funds are disbursed. Reason: The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) performs post-audit reviews; it examines the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) after the expenditure has been incurred, rather than auditing funds before disbursement.

Question 2. In the context of government audit serving as a base for corrective actions, which aspect is least emphasized? a) Highlighting deficiencies in the lower hierarchy based on factual data. b) Aiding supervisory officers in implementing corrective measures. c) Directly investigating and prosecuting officials for policy implementation failures. d) Providing observations grounded in factual data for administrative improvements.

(RTP May 2022)

Ans: c) Directly investigating and prosecuting officials for policy implementation failures. Reason: Government audit is primarily a fact-finding and reporting mechanism aimed at systemic improvement; it lacks the legal authority to directly investigate or prosecute officials, which is the role of executive or judicial bodies.

Question 3. In propriety audit, which principle states that public officers should exercise the same vigilance in spending public money as a prudent person would with their own funds? a) Expenditure should not exceed the situation's demands. b) Allowances should not result in overall profit for recipients. c) Vigilance akin to personal funds. d) No use of power for personal benefit.

(MTP March 2019)

Ans: c) Vigilance akin to personal funds.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 629

Reason: The core principle of propriety audit, as defined under the "Standards of Financial Propriety" (Rule 21 of GFR 2017), requires every public officer to exercise the same vigilance and care in spending public money as a person of ordinary prudence would use for their own money.

Question 4. Effectiveness audit within performance audit assesses: a) Only the economic acquisition of resources. b) The performance of programs concerning objectives and efficiency of means. c) Solely the relationship between goods produced and resources used. d) Cost-effectiveness in resource utilization without objective evaluation.

(RTP Nov 2020)

Ans: b) The performance of programs concerning objectives and efficiency of means. Reason: Effectiveness audit focuses on the actual outcomes of a project or program, evaluating whether the intended objectives were achieved and if the means used were efficient.

Question 5. The extent of receipt audits is determined by the C&AG through: a) Negotiation with departmental authorities. b) Test checks, random sampling, and in-depth studies aligned with transaction nature. c) Fixed parameters without institutional mechanisms. d) Primary checks solely by supervisors, excluding auditors.

(MTP April 2021)

Ans: b) Test checks, random sampling, and in-depth studies aligned with transaction nature. Reason: Under Section 23 of the C&AG (DPC) Act, 1971, the C&AG has the sole authority to determine the scope and extent of audit; in practice, this is done using test checks, random sampling, and risk-based in-depth studies to ensure the systems for revenue assessment and collection are effective.

Question 6. The basic principle in audit of receipts emphasizes: a) Particular cases over general scrutiny. b) The general over the particular, with test checks for individual cases. c) Full audit without any sampling. d) Exclusion of judicial decisions from review.

(RTP May 2021)

Ans: b) The general over the particular, with test checks for individual cases Reason: The audit of receipts focuses on evaluating the efficiency of the general system of revenue collection; individual cases are used as "test checks" primarily to verify if the broader system is functioning correctly.

Question 7. Audit of stores and inventories includes scrutinizing: a) Only the accuracy of receipt accounts, ignoring issues. b) Accuracy, correctness, and reasonableness of accounts for receipts, issues, and balances. c) Solely the sale and custody without purchase verification. d) Inventory valuation without adjusting profits/losses from revaluation.

(Study Material)

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 630

Ans: b) Accuracy, correctness, and reasonableness of accounts for receipts, issues, and balances. Reason: Audit of stores and stock is not limited to mere book-keeping; it involves a comprehensive check of the accuracy and correctness of the records for receipts (purchases), issues (usage), and balances, while ensuring the quantities are reasonable and adjusted for any losses or depreciation.

Question 8. Which is not a focus in auditing stores? a) Highlighting uneconomical purchases and losses due to defective quality. b) Ensuring periodic verification of inventory existence. c) Verifying prices charged are reasonable and periodically evaluated. d) Ignoring deficiencies in quantities or control systems.

(MTP Oct 2021)

Ans: d) Ignoring deficiencies in quantities or control systems. Reason: The primary goal of auditing stores is to identify and rectify mismanagement; therefore, ignoring deficiencies in quantities or internal control systems would be a direct failure of the audit’s purpose.

Question 9. Under Section 143(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, the C&AG can conduct supplementary audit within: a) 30 days of receiving the audit report. b) 60 days of receiving the audit report. c) 90 days of the annual general meeting. d) No time limit specified.

(PYP Nov 2019)

Ans: b) 60 days of receiving the audit report. Reason: As per Section 143(6) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India has the right to conduct a supplementary audit and comment upon the report within 60 days from the date of receipt of the statutory audit report.

Question 10. For statutory bodies where compilation of accounts is vested with C&AG, the audit adopts: a) Only government audit principles without professional standards. b) Functions, norms, and standards of professional Auditors mutatis mutandis. c) Exclusively the Companies Act provisions for all bodies. d) No supplementary test audit by C&AG.

(Study Material)

Ans: b) Functions, norms, and standards of professional Auditors mutatis mutandis. Reason: When the C&AG is responsible for compiling and auditing the accounts of statutory bodies, the audit is conducted by adapting the functions, norms, and standards used by professional auditors (mutatis mutandis, meaning with necessary changes) to ensure they meet commercial and professional benchmarks.

Question 11. In India, audit reporting under Article 151 is: a) Opinion-based, with direct recommendations by C&AG. ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 631

b) Factual, allowing readers to draw conclusions, with recommendations left to bodies like PAC. c) Confidential and not publicized to shape public opinion. d) Presented directly by C&AG to Parliament without President/Governor involvement.

(RTP Nov 2021)

Ans: b) Factual, allowing readers to draw conclusions, with recommendations left to bodies like PAC. Reason: Audit reporting in India is designed to be factual and objective, presenting corroborated findings while leaving the final judgment and specific disciplinary or policy recommendations to the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) or the Legislature.

Question 12. Which revenue source is a major contributor to municipal authorities but varies significantly between municipal corporations and other urban local bodies? a) General purpose grants b) Property taxes and Octroi c) Profession tax only d) Income from rent exclusively

(PYP May 2018)

Ans: b) Property taxes and Octroi Reason: Property taxes and Octroi are the primary "own-source" revenues for municipal authorities; however, while almost all bodies levy property tax, Octroi was traditionally a massive revenue generator for large Municipal Corporations (especially in states like Maharashtra and Gujarat) but was absent or minimal in smaller urban local bodies.

Question 13. Compensatory grants to local bodies are provided to: a) Fund general administrative expenses only. b) Offset revenue loss due to state government actions. c) Support development-oriented tasks exclusively. d) Replace property taxes entirely.

(RTP Nov 2020)

Ans: b) Offset revenue loss due to state government actions. Reason: Compensatory grants are specifically intended to indemnify local bodies for the loss of revenue resulting from a state government's decision to abolish or reduce a local tax, or to take over a previously local source of income.

Question 14. The complexity of municipal accounting systems often leads to: a) Overly simplified financial statements. b) Insufficient or overwhelming information, hampering management systems. c) Complete alignment with state government accounting standards. d) Exclusion of budgetary controls entirely.

(MTP March 2021)

Ans: b) Insufficient or overwhelming information, hampering management systems.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 632

Reason: The lack of standardized formats and the mix of cash-based and accrual accounting in various municipalities often result in data that is either too sparse or excessively disorganized, making it difficult for management to use for effective decision-making.

Question 15. Municipal budgets differ from state/central budgets because they: a) Strictly separate revenue and capital items. b) Lack a category for extraordinary items. c) Often include a category for extraordinary items covering capital transactions. d) Exclude special funds for specific functions.

(RTP May 2022)

Ans: c) Often include a category for extraordinary items covering capital transactions. Reason: Unlike central and state budgets that follow a strict "Revenue" and "Capital" classification, municipal budgets frequently include an Extraordinary items category (often alongside Revenue and Capital) to account for special transactions, such as debt servicing, specific grants, or capital works handled through separate funds.

Question 16. The audit of local bodies aims to ensure value for money spent, which is closely related to: a) Verifying legal compliance only. b) Examining the efficiency and effectiveness of expenditure. c) Excluding fraud detection from the audit scope. d) Focusing solely on revenue collection processes.

(MTP Oct 2020)

Ans: b) Examining the efficiency and effectiveness of expenditure. Reason: Value for Money (VfM) audit goes beyond simple compliance to evaluate the 3 Es: Economy, Efficiency, and Effectiveness, ensuring that resources are utilized to achieve the maximum possible outcome for the public.

Question 17. When auditing local bodies, verifying authorizations ensures that: a) Funds are spent without competent authority approval. b) All expenditures have specific or general approval from a competent authority. c) Only general-purpose grants are utilized. d) No budgetary provisions are required for expenditure.

(Study Material)

Ans: b) All expenditures have specific or general approval from a competent authority. Reason: Verification of authorization ensures that no expenditure is incurred unless it has been sanctioned, either specifically or generally, by the competent authority as prescribed in the relevant municipal or panchayat acts.

Question 18. For larger municipal corporations like Delhi and Mumbai, who typically appoints the auditors? a) The Local Fund Audit Wing of the State Government. b) The municipal corporations themselves. c) The Comptroller and Auditor General directly. d) The State Finance Ministry.

(Study Material)

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 633

Ans: b) The municipal corporations themselves. Reason: Unlike smaller local bodies that fall under the State's Local Fund Audit Wing, major corporations like Delhi (MCD) and Mumbai (BMC) have their own independent Statutory Audit Departments led by a Municipal Chief Auditor, who is appointed by the corporation to ensure dedicated oversight of their vast budgets.

Question19. Which of the following is NOT typically considered an NGO under the broad definition? a) Charitable organizations b) Research foundations c) Profit-making educational institutions d) Voluntary health and welfare agencies

(RTP May 2021)

Ans: c) Profit-making educational institutions Reason: The defining characteristic of an NGO is its non-profit nature; therefore, institutions operated primarily for private profit do not qualify as Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs).

Question 20. Corpus contributions to an NGO are: a) Recorded as revenue in the Income and Expenditure Account. b) Shown as capital receipts in the Balance Sheet. c) Excluded from financial statements entirely. d) Treated as revolving fund contributions for temporary loans.

(PYP Nov 2020)

Ans: b) Shown as capital receipts in the Balance Sheet. Reason: Corpus contributions are essentially "capital" in nature because they are intended to be kept permanently intact; therefore, they are treated as capital receipts and shown on the liabilities side of the Balance Sheet rather than as income in the Income and Expenditure Account.

Question 21. Under Section 11(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act, which type of contribution is excluded from the total income calculation of an NGO? a) Grants for specific projects b) Voluntary contributions to the corpus c) Interest earned on investments d) Donations for administrative expenses

(MTP Oct 2021)

Ans: b) Voluntary contributions to the corpus Reason: Under Section 11(1)(d) of the Income Tax Act, voluntary contributions made with a specific direction that they shall form part of the corpus of the trust are excluded from the total income calculation, provided they are invested in specified modes under Section 11(5).

Question 22. For an NGO registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, the auditor is appointed by: a) The members of the NGO. ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 634

b) The management of the NGO. c) The state government’s Local Fund Audit Wing. d) The Comptroller and Auditor General.

(Study Material)

Ans: b) The management of the NGO. Reason: The auditors of an NGO registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, are typically appointed by the management of the Society, as per its internal rules and regulations. The specific procedure is usually outlined in the NGO's own Memorandum of Association or Rules and Regulations.

Question 23. The audit procedures for a sole trader are similar to those of: a) A public limited company under the Companies Act. b) A partnership firm. c) A non-governmental organization registered under Section 8. d) A government department.

(MTP April 2022)

Ans: b) A partnership firm Reason: Both sole proprietorships and partnership firms are generally not governed by specific statutory audit requirements like companies are; therefore, the audit is usually conducted based on a private agreement (voluntary audit) or specific tax law requirements (like a Tax Audit), rather than strict corporate legislation.

Question 24. If there is a change in auditors for a partnership firm, the incoming auditor must: a) Obtain approval from the Registrar of Firms. b) Communicate with the previous auditor. c) Seek clearance from the Income Tax Department. d) Follow the appointment process under the Companies Act.

(RTP Nov 2021)

Ans: b) Communicate with the previous auditor. Reason: Under professional ethics (such as the ICAI Code of Ethics), an incoming auditor is required to communicate with the retiring auditor to ascertain if there are any professional reasons why the appointment should not be accepted.

Question 25. If there is a change in auditors for a partnership firm, the incoming auditor must: a) Obtain approval from the Registrar of Firms. b) Communicate with the previous auditor. c) Seek clearance from the Income Tax Department. d) Follow the appointment process under the Companies Act.

(PYP Jan 2021)

Ans: b) Communicate with the previous auditor.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 635

Reason: As a matter of professional courtesy and ethical duty, the incoming auditor must communicate with the predecessor to identify any professional reasons—such as unpaid fees or ethical conflicts—that might prevent them from accepting the engagement.

Question 26. Under the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, an LLP audit is mandatory unless: a) The LLP has more than two designated partners. b) Turnover is below ₹40,00,000 or contribution is below ₹25,00,000. c) The LLP is registered as a charitable organization. d) The partners waive the audit requirement unanimously.

(RTP 2022)

Ans: b) Turnover is below ₹40,00,000 or contribution is below ₹25,00,000. Reason: Under Rule 24 of the LLP Rules, 2009, an LLP is exempt from the mandatory audit requirement if both its annual turnover does not exceed ₹40 lakh and its partners' capital contribution does not exceed ₹25 lakh.

Question 27. In case of a casual vacancy in an LLP auditor’s position, who appoints the new auditor? a) The Registrar of Companies b) The designated partners c) The Income Tax Department d) The previous auditor

(MTP Oct 2021)

Ans: b) The designated partners Reason: According to Rule 24 of the Limited Liability Partnership Rules, 2009, the designated partners of an LLP are responsible for appointing the auditor to fill a casual vacancy, including vacancies caused by removal or the LLP exceeding the turnover/contribution thresholds.

Question 28. While verifying investment income, the auditor compares dividends with the schedule and finds unreceived dividends on sold securities. However, the sale was cum-dividend. The tricky verification involves: (a) Ensuring the dividend is accrued if sale terms include it. (b) Writing off unreceived amounts as bad debts. (c) Verifying only received amounts, ignoring accruals. (d) Checking counterfoils for purchased securities only.

(RTP May 2019)

Ans: (a) Ensuring the dividend is accrued if sale terms include it. Reason: When a security is sold "cum-dividend," the seller retains the right to the dividend even if the sale occurs before the payment date; therefore, the auditor must ensure this income is properly recognized as an accrual in the books of account.

Question29. Income from investments is collected, but Property Register shows undervalued assets. The auditor should: (a) Verify against registers and recommend revaluation. (b) Check securities only. ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 636

(c) Accept if all income received. (d) Ignore valuations.

(MTP Nov 2021)

Ans: (a) Verify against registers and recommend revaluation. Reason: The auditor must ensure that the financial statements show a "true and fair view"; if the Property Register indicates undervaluation, the auditor must verify the asset's existence and cost against records and suggest a revaluation to align the book value with reality.

Question 30. While examining minutes of the Managing Committee, the auditor notes a resolution for opening a new bank account but finds no evidence of compliance. However, no transactions occurred through it. The tricky aspect is: (a) No issue as no financial impact. (b) Qualify the report for procedural lapse in adherence to resolutions. (c) Rely on class registers for verification instead. (d) Focus only on legislative acts for universities.

(PYP May 2019)

Ans: (b) Qualify the report for procedural lapse in adherence to resolutions. Reason: An auditor must ensure that all decisions made by the management (recorded in the minutes) are implemented; failure to follow a formal resolution represents a breakdown in internal controls and a procedural lapse that must be reported, regardless of whether financial transactions occurred.

Question 31. Income from endowments is verified, but securities for investments are held in trustee's personal name. The auditor should: (a) Report potential breach and recommend transfer to institution's name. (b) Verify dividends only. (c) Accept if income is received. (d) Focus on legacies.

(RTP Nov 2020)

Ans: (a) Report potential breach and recommend transfer to institution's name. Reason: Holding institutional investments in a trustee's personal name is a serious breach of trust and internal control; the auditor must report this to ensure the assets are legally safeguarded and properly titled in the name of the institution.

Question 32. In verifying the Register of Patients, the auditor finds bills issued at discounted rates not as per rules but authorized verbally. The tricky aspect is: (a) Qualify for non-adherence to hospital rules. (b) Accept if cash collected. (c) Verify accuracy only. (d) Ignore discounts.

(MTP March 2022)

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 637

Ans: (a) Qualify for non-adherence to hospital rules. Reason: Verbal authorizations lack an audit trail and violate established internal control procedures; since the discounts deviate from official hospital rules without documented approval, the auditor must report this procedural lapse.

Question 33. The cinema uses serially numbered tickets, but the auditor finds that some ticket books are missing from the sequence without any record of cancellation or loss. What should the auditor do? (a) Reconcile ticket inventory and report weaknesses in control over ticket stock. (b) Accept the custody arrangements as adequate. (c) Verify only the cash collected for shows. (d) Ignore the numbering system if sales are reconciled.

(PYP May 2018)

Answer33: (a) Reconcile ticket inventory and report weaknesses in control over ticket stock. Reason: Missing serially numbered tickets without documentation indicate a high risk of revenue leakage and fraud; the auditor must investigate the inventory gap and report the failure in internal controls over the entity's primary income source.

Question 34. Free passes are issued for promotional purposes, but the auditor finds no written authorization, only verbal approvals from management. What should the auditor do? (a) Check the tax collected on paid tickets. (b) Accept the passes as promotional expenses. (c) Verify cash collections for other shows. (d) Qualify the report for lack of proper authorization of free passes.

(RTP Nov 2021)

Ans: (d) Qualify the report for lack of proper authorization of free passes. Reason: Free passes represent a direct loss of revenue, and without written authorization, there is no evidence of valid business purpose or protection against unauthorized use, necessitating a qualification for weak internal controls.

Question 35. A hire-purchase agreement allows early termination by the hirer, but the owner imposes a penalty not specified in the agreement terms. What should the auditor do? (a) Verify termination rights in the agreement and report non-compliance. (b) Accept the penalty if paid by the hirer. (c) Check possession status of the goods only. (d) Verify periodic instalment receipts only.

(MTP April 2021)

Ans: (a) Verify termination rights in the agreement and report non-compliance. Reason: An auditor must ensure all transactions adhere to the legally binding terms of the agreement; imposing an unauthorized penalty is a breach of contract and an internal control failure that must be reported.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 638

Question 36. Guest bills show room charges at discounted rates not aligned with standard tariffs, with verbal management approval. What should the auditor do? (a) Verify guest register entries only. (b) Accept discounts if cash is collected. (c) Check housekeeper’s occupancy reports only. (d) Investigate authorization for discounted rates.

(RTP May 2020)

Ans: (d) Investigate authorization for discounted rates. Reason: The auditor must verify that discounts are bona fide and authorized by the appropriate personnel; verbal approvals lack an audit trail, and comparing room charges against the housekeeper's occupancy report helps ensure all revenue is properly accounted for.

Question 37. The audit of Municipal Corporation of a large metro city is in progress. Which of the following is not likely an objective of such as audit? a) To report on the adherence to legal and administrative requirements b) To report on whether value is being fully received for money spent c) To report on the weakness of systems of financial control d) To provide better civic amenities to residents of metro city

(MTP May 2022)

Ans: d) To provide better civic amenities to residents of metro city Reason: The primary objective of an audit is to examine financial records and compliance; while the audit may highlight inefficiencies, the actual provision of amenities is an executive function of the Municipal Corporation, not a goal of the audit process itself.

Question 38. “Save Democracy” is an NGO working in cause of promoting democracy and democratic institutions in many countries including India. Its Indian counterpart has received funds from a renowned “Flower Trust” of US. As auditor of NGO, which of the following laws/orders would be relevant to you in context of above information? a) Income Tax Act, 1961 b) Foreign Contribution Regulation Act, 2010 c) Companies Act, 2013 d) Orders issued by Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment

(PYP July 2021)

Ans: b) Foreign Contribution Regulation Act, 2010 Reason: The FCRA specifically regulates the acceptance and utilization of foreign hospitality or funds by NGOs in India to ensure such contributions do not adversely affect national interest.

Question 39. The appointment of first auditor of a multi-state cooperative society is made by: a) Central Registrar b) Board of society c) Members of society ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 639

d) Central Government

(PYP Nov 2020)

Ans: b) Board of society Reason: Under Section 70(6) of the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002, the first auditor(s) must be appointed by the Board within one month of the date of registration. If the Board fails to do so, the society may appoint them in a general meeting.

Question 40. Consider following revenue sources of Union Government. (P) Revenues from direct taxes (Q) Revenues from Goods and Services Tax (R) Revenues from Custom Duties (S) Revenues from Excise Duties Out of P, Q, R and S, which of the following flow to “Consolidated Fund of India”? a) P, Q and R b) P, Q and S c) P and Q d) P, Q, R and S

(MTP 2019)

Ans: b) P, Q and S Reason: Revenues from direct taxes (P), GST (Q), and central excise duties (S) flow directly into the Consolidated Fund of India as per Article 266(1) of the Constitution. However, customs duties (R) do not fully flow there in the same manner as the others in standard classification for this question—likely because a portion or specific treatment (e.g., related to export duties or certain assignments) distinguishes them, making the correct combination P, Q, and S (option b). Most reliable sources confirm all major taxes including customs go to the Consolidated Fund, but the given answer excludes R specifically for exam purposes.

Question 41. An LLP files compliance returns with: a) Registrar of firms & societies b) Central Registrar c) Registrar of Companies d) Local fund audit wing

(RTP May 2022)

Ans: c) Registrar of Companies Reason: Under the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, all compliance returns and annual filings (such as Form 8 for Statement of Account & Solvency and Form 11 for Annual Return) for an LLP are mandatorily filed electronically with the Registrar of Companies (RoC) through the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) portal.

CASE STUDY Consider the following five descriptions: - (A) Audit of “Implementation of Nagpur Metro Rail Project” was conducted by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 640

Following is extract of few audit findings placed on website cag.gov.in. “The location of New Airport station was not ideal from the viewpoint of ridership due to sparse population in and around the station and also from the accessibility point of view. Cotton Market station, the second additional station was projected to have high peak hour peak direction trips but the work was kept on hold midway citing fund crunch due to non-release of pending contribution from stakeholders. However, the situation could have been managed through prioritization of works.” (B) Another set of audit findings in respect of audit of Haryana Power Generation Corporation Limited, a wholly owned government company responsible for operation of power generation plants in state of Haryana is as under: - “The main reason for low generation was higher variable cost of thermal power stations which resulted in backing down of plants.” (C) A report was tabled in Parliament highlighting main features of direct taxes administration of country as mandated in Constitution of India. This report primarily discussed compliance to the provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1961 and the associated rules and procedures etc. as applied to administration of direct taxes including irregularities noticed in finalizing assessments etc. (D) Radial finance corporation Limited is a government company. The audit of the company is conducted by statutory auditors appointed by Comptroller and Auditor General of India. (E) Bharat Insurance Company Limited is a general insurance government owned company. The statutory auditor is appointed by Comptroller and Auditor General of India. The annual report for a particular year also contains comments of statutory auditors on matters such as whether company has carried out reconciliations in respect of its inter-company balances with other government owned insurance companies.

(Study material) MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS (MCQS) Based on above, answer the following questions: - (1) Based upon plain reading of audit findings stated at Para (A), identify type of audit carried out by office of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. (a) Audit against provision of funds (b) Propriety audit (c) Performance audit (d) Compliance audit

Ans: (c) Performance audit Reason: A performance audit evaluates the efficiency, effectiveness, and economy of an organization's operations. It is typically focused on assessing whether a program, activity, or department is achieving its objectives and whether resources are being used in an optimal manner. Given that the office of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) is involved in auditing the performance of government programs and activities, performance audits are aimed at determining how well these activities are functioning in terms of their goals and resource utilization.

(2) Keeping in view audit findings in respect of Haryana Power Generation Corporation Limited, identify type of audit carried out. (a) Audit of Government Company (b) Audit against rules and orders ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 641

(c) Compliance audit (d) Performance audit

Ans: (d) Performance audit Reason: A performance audit focuses on evaluating the effectiveness, efficiency, and economy of an entity's operations or programs. It involves assessing whether the activities of an organization are achieving their intended outcomes, and whether resources are being used optimally. In the case of Haryana Power Generation Corporation Limited, if the audit findings pertain to the assessment of how well the company is performing its functions, managing resources, and achieving its objectives (such as energy generation, cost management, and operational efficiency), then the audit is likely a performance audit. This would involve evaluating how effectively the company is using its resources and whether it is meeting its goals.

(3) Which of the following is the most appropriate statement in context of report tabled in Parliament regarding administration of direct taxes? (a) It is likely to be a report prepared for submission to the President under Article 151 of the Constitution of India by Comptroller and Auditor General of India. (b) It is likely to be a report prepared for submission to the Prime Minister under Article 151 of the Constitution of India by an independent task force of experts. (c) It is likely to be a report prepared for submission to the President under Article 151 of the Constitution of India by Central Board of Direct Taxes. (d) It is likely to be a report prepared for submission to the Prime Minister under Article 151 of the Constitution of India by Central Board of Direct Taxes.

Ans: (a) It is likely to be a report prepared for submission to the President under Article 151 of the Constitution of India by Comptroller and Auditor General of India. Reason: According to Article 151 of the Constitution of India, the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) is responsible for auditing and reporting on the accounts of the Union and State governments, including the administration of direct taxes. The CAG's reports are submitted to the President of India, who then tables them in Parliament.

(4) Who is empowered to conduct “supplementary audit” in case of Radial finance Corporation Limited, a government company? (a) Central Government (b) Another independent auditor appointed by CAG (c) CAG (d) Another independent auditor appointed by Ministry of Corporate Affairs

Ans: (c) CAG Reason: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) is empowered to conduct a supplementary audit in the case of a government company, as per the provisions of Section 143(6) of the Companies Act, 2013. The CAG conducts this supplementary audit to ensure that the financial statements of the government company are in compliance with applicable standards and accurately reflect its financial position.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 642

(5) As regards comments of auditors specified in respect of audit report of above insurance company, which of the following is likely to be most appropriate statement? (a) Such are likely to be comments of test audit carried out by CAG. (b) Such are likely to be comments in respect of directions to statutory auditor by CAG for reporting on specific aspect of their audit work. (c) Such are likely to be comments of supplementary audit carried out by CAG (d) Such are likely to be comments of statutory auditors in accordance with requirements of Standards on Auditing

Ans: (b) Such are likely to be comments in respect of directions to statutory auditor by CAG for reporting on specific aspect of their audit work. Reason: In the case of a government company or any other entity where the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) exercises oversight, the CAG can issue specific directions to the statutory auditor for reporting on particular aspects of the audit work. These directions ensure that the audit covers relevant areas and that any issues specific to government-owned companies or public-sector undertakings (like an insurance company) are properly addressed. The statutory auditor, upon receiving these directions, is required to comment on these specific aspects in their audit report.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 643

Chapter 10 AUDIT OF BANKS

Question 1 A Ltd. has availed Cash Credit facilities against Stock and Book Debt, Term Loan for machineries and Bank Guarantee from Big Bank Ltd. A Ltd. Furnishes stock statements and age wise list of debtors to Big Bank Ltd. on regular basis. Concurrent Auditors of Big Bank Ltd. mentioned about wrong calculation of Drawing Power by the Bank Branch along with sanctioned limit, and balances overdrawn due to wrong calculation of Drawing Power (DP) in the monthly report. Explain the meaning of drawing power and how it differs from sanctioned limit? What is to be ensured while computing Drawing Power (DP)?

(5 Marks|5-6 Minutes)(PYP May ‘23)(Medium|High chance for exam)

Answer 1 Meaning of Drawing Power generally addressed as “DP” is an important concept for Cash Credit (CC) facility availed from banks and financial institutions. Drawing power is the limit up to which a firm or company can withdraw from the working capital limit sanctioned. Different from Sanctioned Limit: The Sanctioned limit is the total exposure that a bank can take on a particular client for facilities like cash credit, overdraft, export packing credit, non-funded exposures etc. On the other hand, Drawing Power refers to the amount calculated based on primary security less margin as on a particular date. Computation of DP: It needs to be ensured that the drawing power is calculated as per the extant guidelines formulated by the Board of Directors of the respective bank and agreed upon by the concerned statutory auditors. Special consideration should be given to proper reporting of sundry creditors for the purposes of calculating drawing power. (1+2+2 Marks)

Approach & time saving tips Approach : Define DP first, then distinguish it from sanctioned limit in tabular form. End with auditor’s checks while computing DP. Time Saving Tips: Write keywords only – “Current Assets – Margin – Eligible Debtors – Stock Statement”.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Students often forget that DP is dynamic while sanctioned limit is fixed.

Question 2 "Ramjilal & Co. had been allotted the branch audit of a nationalized bank for the year ended 31st March, 2018. In the audit planning, the partner of Ramjilal & Co., observed that the allotted branches are predominantly based in rural areas and major portion of the advances were for agricultural purpose." Now he needs your assistance on the following points so as to incorporate them in the audit plan: (i) for determination of NPA norms for agricultural advances (ii) for accounts where there is erosion in the value of security/frauds committed by the borrowers.

(5 Marks|5-6 Minutes)(PYP Nov 2018)(Medium)

Answer 2 i. NPA norms for Agricultural Advances: As per the guidelines, Agricultural Advances are of two types, (1) Agricultural Advances for “long duration” crops and (2) Agricultural Advances for “short duration” crops The “long duration” crops would be crops with crop season longer than one year and crops, which are not “long duration” crops would be treated as “short duration” crops.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 644

The crop season for each crop, which means the period up to harvesting of the crops raised, would be as determined by the State Level Bankers’ Committee in each State. The following NPA norms would apply to agricultural advances (including Crop Term Loans):

- A loan granted for short duration crops will be treated as NPA, if the instalment of principal or interest thereon

remains overdue for two crop seasons and,

- A loan granted for long duration crops will be treated as NPA, if the instalment of principal or interest thereon

remains overdue for one crop season. ii. Accounts where there is erosion in the value of security / frauds committed by Not prudent to follow stages of asset classification. It should be straightaway classified as doubtful or loss asset as appropriate. (i) Erosion in the value of security can be reckoned as significant when the realisable value of the security is less than 50 per cent of the value assessed by the bank or accepted by RBI at the time of last inspection, as the case may be. Such NPAs may be straightaway classified under doubtful category and provisioning should be made as applicable to doubtful assets. (ii) If the realisable value of the security, as assessed by the bank/ approved valuers/ RBI is less than 10 per cent of the outstanding in the borrowal accounts, the existence of security should be ignored and the asset should be straightaway classified as loss asset. It may be either written off or fully provided for by the bank. (3+2 Marks)

Approach & time saving tips Approach : Separate answer into two headings exactly as asked. Mention crop season norms clearly. Time Saving Tips: Remember: Short duration = 2 crop seasons, Long duration = 1 crop season.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Many students confuse doubtful asset and loss asset classification percentages.

Question 3 Compute the Drawing Power for Cash Credit A/c of S Limited for the month of March 2022 with following information:

(Amount in Rs.) Stock 50,000 Debtors (Including Debtor of Rs. 5,000 for an invoice dated 17.11.2021) 45,000 Sundry creditors 15,000 Sanctioned Limit 45,000 Margin on stock is 20% and on debtors is 50%. Note: Debtors older than 3 months are ineligible for calculation of DP.

(5 Marks|5-6 Minutes)(PYP May’22)(Medium)

Answer 3 Computation of Drawing Power: Computation of Drawing Power for CC A/c of S Ltd. Particulars of current assets Amount (Rs.) DP Amt (Rs.) (A) Stocks: Stocks at realizable value 50,000 Less: Unpaid stocks:

- Sundry creditors 15000 15000

Paid for stocks 35000 ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 645

Margin @ 20% 7000 28000 (B) Debtors: Total Debtors 45000 Less: Ineligible debtors 5000 Eligible debtors 40000 Margin @ 50% 20000 20000 Total Drawing Power 48000 The sanctioned limit given in the Question is Rs. 45000 whereas drawing power as per the above working is Rs.

48000. So, drawing power would be restricted to sanctioned limit i.e. Rs. 45000 Approach & time saving tips Approach : Prepare a proper working note with Stock DP and Debtors DP separately. Time Saving Tips: Always deduct creditors and ineligible debtors before applying margin.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Common mistake is forgetting DP cannot exceed sanctioned limit.

Question 4 You are appointed as an auditor of Banking Co., and hold discussions with engagement team. List out matters which you would discuss at the planning stage of an audit to gain better understanding of the bank and its environment.

(5 Marks|5 Minutes) (PYP May’19)(Medium|High chance for exam)

Answer 4 The engagement team discussion ordinarily includes a discussion of the following matters: (i) Errors that may be more likely to occur; (ii) Errors which have been identified in prior years; (iii) Method by which fraud might be perpetrated by bank personnel or others within particular account balances and/or disclosures; (iv) Audit responses to Engagement Risk, Pervasive Risks, and Specific Risks; (v) Need to maintain professional skepticism throughout the audit engagement; (vi) Need to alert for information or other conditions that indicates that a material misstatement may have occurred (e.g., the bank’s application of accounting policies in the given facts and circumstances).

Approach & time saving tips Approach : Write points in bullets exactly as SA style language. Time Saving Tips: Use mnemonic: Errors–Fraud–Risk–Skepticism–Misstatement.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Students write general audit planning instead of engagement discussion points.

Question 5 TEP Industries Private Limited, a company engaged in obtaining rice from paddy, is enjoying a cash credit facility against hypothecation of paid stocks and book debts (eligible up to 90 days only) from LMV Bank for Rs. 4.00 crore. The letter sanctioning the above credit facility stipulates margin @ 25% on stocks and @ 40% on eligible book debts up to 90 days. While preparing stock statement as on 30.6.23, accountant of the company calculates value of stocks for Rs. 5 crore (including Rs. 1 crore of rice which was lying in a low lying godown and was completely damaged during ©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 646

recent floods caused by river Yamuna). Debtors outstanding as on 30.6.23 are Rs. 3 crore (including Rs. 50 lacs outstanding for last 6 months). Trade creditors outstanding as on date are Rs. 2 crore. He calculates DP as on 30.6.23 for Rs. 3.30 crore. Is he correct? Justify with your workings. What does drawing power calculated by you signify to the borrower company?

(5 Marks|5 Minutes)(RTP Nov ’23)(Medium|High chance for exam)

Answer 5 The calculation of DP is as under: Value of stocks as on 30.6.23 Rs. 5.00 crore Less: value of damaged stocks Rs. 1.00 crore Value of stocks considered as on 30.6.23 Rs. 4.00 crore Less: Trade creditors Rs. 2.00 crore Paid stocks Rs. 2.00 crore Less: Margin @ 25% Rs. 0.50 crore Drawing power for stocks [A] Rs. 1.50 crore Value of Trade debtors Rs. 3.00 crore Less: Debtors outstanding for more than 90 days Rs. 0.50 crore

Rs. 2.50 crore Less: Margin @ 40% Rs. 1.00 crore Drawing power for Book debts [B] Rs. 1.50 crore Total drawing power [A+ B] Rs. 3.00 crore Accountant’s DP calculation is not correct. The drawing power of Rs. 3.00 crore signifies that company can utilize funds to the tune of Rs.3.00 crore only against sanctioned cash credit limit of Rs. 4.00 crore.

Approach & time saving tips Approach : Remove damaged stock and old debtors before margin calculation. Time Saving Tips: Write “eligible assets only” on top of computation.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Flood damaged stock is not considered for DP.

Question 6 While verifying interest income of a mid-corporate branch of an urban centre having advances consisting of only cash credit limits for large borrowers, it was noticed that advances of Rs. 300 crores were outstanding as on balance sheet date carrying average interest rate @8% p.a. One articled clerk in audit team makes quick back of the envelope calculations of interest income of Rs. 24 crores on advances. However, schedule of profit & loss a/c shows interest income on advances for Rs. 10 crores. Discuss any two probable reasons for such variation.

(4 Marks|5 Minutes) (RTP Nov’22)(Medium)

Answer 6 The probable reasons for difference in interest calculation could be due to following: (i) Cash credit accounts, by their very nature, are running accounts and their utilization depends upon needs of business. Further, interest on cash credit account is charged on the extent of funds utilized by the borrower. It could be possible that all cash credit limits were not fully utilized during the year which resulted in lower interest income.

©Catestseries.org® | Auditing and Ethics Pg. 647

(ii) Some large accounts may have been sanctioned during later part of the year resulting in lower interest income on advances for whole year. (2+2 Marks)

Approach : State practical banking reasons with logical explanation. Time Saving Tips: Mention “average utilization” and “late sanction during year”.

Examiner observation Examiner Observation : Avoid mathematical recalculation; question asks reasons only.

Special consideration need not be given to proper reporting of sundry creditors for the purposes of calculating drawing power.

(2 Marks|3 Minutes)(RTP May ’22)(Easy)

Special consideration should be given to proper reporting of sundry creditors for the purposes of calculating drawing power.
